What the assumption costs is calibration: correlated features get counted as independent evidence, so the posterior is pushed toward zero or one far more than the data justify. Scikit-learn's calibration guide shows exactly this overconfidence for Gaussian naive Bayes. So if I need probabilities, for thresholds or expected costs, I'd calibrate it on held out data or switch to logistic regression, which learns the same linear form without the independence assumption.
must_mention: only the argmax must be right

followups.q: How would you calibrate it?
followups.a: CalibratedClassifierCV with sigmoid or isotonic regression on held out folds.

followups.q: When is naive Bayes the right choice?
followups.a: Very small labelled sets, text with huge vocabularies, or when training speed matters.

traps: Trusting naive Bayes probabilities as calibrated risk scores.

topic: kNN and the curse of dimensionality
q: How does the k nearest neighbours algorithm work, and what does it cost?
plain: The k nearest neighbours algorithm (kNN) predicts for a new point by finding the k training points closest to it and letting them vote. For regression, the algorithm averages their values. There is no training step at all: the model is just the stored data. With k equal to 5, a new loan applicant is labelled risky if at least 3 of the 5 most similar past applicants defaulted. The price is paid at prediction time, because every prediction must measure distance to many stored points. The result also depends entirely on how distance is defined.
deep:
Prediction: $\hat y(x) = \text{mode}\{y_i : i \in N_k(x)\}$ (classification) or $\frac1k\sum_{i\in N_k(x)}y_i$ (regression); optionally weight by $1/\text{distance}$.

Costs: training $O(1)$ beyond storage; prediction $O(nd)$ by brute force; KD trees and ball trees give roughly $O(\log n)$ queries in low dimensions but degrade as $d$ grows; approximate nearest neighbour indexes (HNSW, IVF) serve embeddings at scale. Memory $O(nd)$.

Design choices: distance (Euclidean, Manhattan, cosine), feature scaling (essential), $k$, weighting. It is nonparametric and makes no assumption about the boundary's shape.
say: kNN is a lazy, nonparametric method: training just stores the data, and to predict for a new point I find the k closest training points under some distance and take a majority vote, or an average for regression, possibly weighted by distance. All the cost is at prediction time, order n times d per query by brute force, which is why large systems use tree indexes in low dimensions or approximate nearest neighbour indexes for embeddings. Its behaviour depends entirely on the distance metric, so I always scale features first. It makes no assumption about the boundary's shape, which is its strength, and it suffers badly in high dimensions, which is its weakness.
must_mention: vote or average of k nearest
order n times d per query
distance metric and scaling decide everything

followups.q: How do you speed up kNN queries?
followups.a: KD trees or ball trees in low dimensions, approximate nearest neighbour indexes like HNSW in high dimensions, or condensing the training set.

followups.q: What distance for text embeddings?
followups.a: Usually cosine similarity, often on normalised vectors so it matches Euclidean ranking.

topic: kNN and the curse of dimensionality
q: How do you choose k in k nearest neighbours, and how does k affect bias and variance?
plain: Small k follows individual points closely, and large k averages over many points. With k of 1, every training point is classified correctly. But one mislabelled point carves out its own little region, so variance is high. Large k smooths the boundary, so variance falls and bias rises. With k equal to the whole dataset, the model predicts the majority class everywhere. Choose k by cross validation. Prefer an odd k for two classes to avoid ties, and scale features first because distance drives everything.
deep:
- $k = 1$: zero training error, jagged boundary, high variance (asymptotically still competitive).
- $k = n$: constant prediction, maximum bias.
- Effective degrees of freedom roughly $n/k$, so complexity falls as $k$ rises.

Selection: CV over a grid, often up to about $\sqrt{n}$; odd $k$ for binary votes; distance weighting reduces sensitivity to $k$. Preprocessing: standardise features; choose a metric suited to the data. In high dimensions reduce dimension first.
say: k is the bias variance knob. With k equals one, each training point gets its own little region, training error is zero and the boundary is jagged, so variance is high. As k grows, each prediction averages more neighbours, the boundary smooths, variance drops and bias rises, until at k equals n I predict the majority class everywhere. I'd pick k by cross validation over a range, use an odd k for binary problems to avoid ties, and often weight votes by distance so k matters less. Before any of that I'd standardise the features, because a feature measured in large units would dominate the distance.

followups.q: What happens when you increase or decrease k?
followups.a: Increasing k smooths the boundary and raises bias; decreasing it makes predictions follow individual points.

followups.q: How does k impact bias and variance?
followups.a: Variance falls and bias rises as k grows.

traps: Choosing k on the test set.

source.title: Chip Huyen, ML Interviews Book, classic ML questions

topic: kNN and the curse of dimensionality
q: What is the curse of dimensionality, and why do we care?
plain: The curse of dimensionality means that as the number of features grows, data points end up far apart and almost equally far from each other. The space becomes so vast that data cannot fill it. In a simulation with 500 random points, the nearest point was about 40 times closer than the farthest in 2 dimensions. In 1,000 dimensions, the nearest point was 90 percent as far as the farthest. To capture 10 percent of the data in 100 dimensions, you need a box spanning 98 percent of each feature's range. That box is hardly local. So distance based methods lose meaning, and the data needed to cover the space grows exponentially.
deep:
Verified (500 uniform points in the unit cube, one query):

| $d$ | nearest / farthest distance | edge of sub cube holding 10% of volume ($0.1^{1/d}$) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | 0.024 | 0.316 |
| 10 | 0.177 | 0.794 |
| 100 | 0.737 | 0.977 |
| 1000 | 0.904 | 0.998 |

Consequences: kNN, kernel methods and clustering degrade; density estimation needs exponentially many samples; overfitting risk rises with $d$ relative to $n$; most volume of a high dimensional ball lies near its surface.

Mitigations: real data concentrate near low dimensional manifolds; use feature selection, PCA, regularisation, learned embeddings, or models like trees that split on one feature at a time.
say: It's the set of problems that appear when the number of dimensions is large relative to the data. The most intuitive one is distance concentration: in a quick simulation with 500 random points, the nearest neighbour was about forty times closer than the farthest point in two dimensions, but in a thousand dimensions the nearest was ninety percent as far as the farthest, so nearest stops meaning much. Also, to capture ten percent of the data in a hundred dimensions you need a box covering ninety eight percent of every feature's range. It hurts kNN, clustering and kernels. The saving grace is that real data usually live near a lower dimensional structure, so dimensionality reduction helps.
must_mention: real data lie near low dimensional manifolds

followups.q: How does it relate to overfitting?
followups.a: With many features per row, flexible models can fit noise; regularisation and selection reduce the effective dimension.

followups.q: Why do embeddings still work for similarity search?
followups.a: Learned embeddings concentrate meaningful variation in structured directions, so relative similarity stays informative.

source.title: Alexey Grigorev, data science interview theory questions

q: What is the margin of a linear classifier? Distinguish the functional margin from the geometric margin.
plain: The margin is how far a correctly classified point sits from the decision boundary. A point far from the boundary is a confident prediction, and one right next to it is fragile. The functional margin is the raw score times the label. You can inflate the functional margin just by doubling all the weights, without changing any prediction. The geometric margin divides by the length of the weight vector, giving the actual distance to the boundary. The geometric margin does not change with rescaling. Support vector machines (SVMs) choose the boundary that maximises the smallest geometric margin over the training set.
deep:
Labels $y \in \{-1, +1\}$, classifier $\mathrm{sign}(w^\top x + b)$ (CS229 sections 6.1 to 6.3).
- Functional margin: $\hat\gamma_i = y_i(w^\top x_i + b)$; scaling $(w, b) \to (2w, 2b)$ doubles it without changing predictions.
- Geometric margin: $\gamma_i = y_i\big(\frac{w^\top x_i + b}{\lVert w\rVert}\big)$, the signed Euclidean distance to the hyperplane $w^\top x + b = 0$ ($w$ is normal to the hyperplane).
- Margin of the training set: $\gamma = \min_i\gamma_i$. When $\lVert w\rVert = 1$ the two coincide.

The scale invariance of the geometric margin lets us impose any normalisation, which is what turns margin maximisation into a convex problem.
say: The margin is the distance from a point to the decision boundary, signed so that it's positive when the point is classified correctly. The functional margin is y times w transpose x plus b, which measures confidence, but it's scale dependent: doubling w and b doubles it without changing a single prediction. The geometric margin divides by the norm of w, giving the true Euclidean distance to the hyperplane, which is invariant to rescaling. The margin of a dataset is the smallest margin over its points. SVMs maximise that smallest geometric margin, and the scale freedom is exactly what lets us fix the functional margin to one and get a convex problem.
must_mention: geometric margin divides by norm of w

followups.q: Why is w orthogonal to the hyperplane?
followups.a: For any two points on the hyperplane, w transpose their difference is zero.

followups.q: Why prefer a large margin?
followups.a: Small perturbations of the data or boundary do not flip predictions, and margin based bounds suggest better generalisation.

source.title: Stanford CS229 main notes, Spring 2026

q: Derive the hard margin SVM optimisation problem and the margin width two over the norm of w.
plain: The hard margin SVM (support vector machine) is derived from one wish. The wish is to find the boundary that maximises the smallest distance from any training point to it, with every point on its correct side. You can rescale the weights freely without moving the boundary. So you can choose the scale so the closest points have a raw score of exactly plus or minus 1. Then the distance from the boundary to those closest points is one over the length of the weight vector. So maximising the margin is the same as minimising the weight vector's length. The gap between the two sides is two over that length.
deep:
Start: $\max_{\gamma, w, b}\ \gamma$ s.t. $y_i(w^\top x_i + b) \ge \gamma$, $\lVert w\rVert = 1$ (non convex constraint).
Equivalent: $\max \hat\gamma/\lVert w\rVert$ s.t. $y_i(w^\top x_i + b) \ge \hat\gamma$ (non convex objective).
Fix the scale with $\hat\gamma = 1$; maximising $1/\lVert w\rVert$ equals minimising $\lVert w\rVert^2$:
$$\min_{w,b}\ \tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\quad\text{s.t.}\quad y_i(w^\top x_i + b) \ge 1,\ i = 1..n.$$
A convex quadratic objective with linear constraints: a QP with a unique solution (CS229 section 6.4).

Width: the hyperplanes $w^\top x + b = \pm1$ are each $1/\lVert w\rVert$ from $w^\top x + b = 0$, so the street is $2/\lVert w\rVert$ wide. Verified: with $C = 0.01$ the fitted margin width was 2.62; with $C = 1$, 1.15.
say: I want to maximise the minimum geometric margin, that is gamma, subject to every point having y times the score at least gamma and w having unit norm. The unit norm constraint is non convex, so I use the scale freedom instead: rescale w and b so the functional margin of the closest points is exactly one. Then the geometric margin is one over the norm of w, and maximising it is the same as minimising one half the squared norm of w, subject to y times w transpose x plus b being at least one for every point. That's a convex quadratic program. The two supporting hyperplanes sit at plus and minus one, so the street is two over the norm of w wide.
must_mention: minimise half squared norm of w
width two over norm of w

followups.q: Why is the result convex?
followups.a: The objective is a convex quadratic and every constraint is linear in w and b.

followups.q: What if the data are not separable?
followups.a: No feasible point exists; add slack variables, the soft margin SVM.

source.title: Stanford CS229 main notes, Spring 2026

q: What does the C parameter do in a soft margin SVM?
plain: The C parameter in a soft margin SVM (support vector machine) sets the price of each margin violation. Real data usually cannot be split perfectly, so the soft margin SVM lets some points sit inside the margin or on the wrong side, at a cost. A small C makes violations cheap, so the model keeps a wide, forgiving margin that ignores some points. A small C means more bias and less variance. A large C makes violations expensive, so the model narrows the margin to classify nearly every training point correctly. A large C means less bias and more variance. In one test, C of 0.01 gave a margin of 2.62 with 134 support vectors (the points that define the boundary). In the same test, C of 1 gave a margin of 1.15 with 58 support vectors.
deep:
$$\min_{w,b,\xi}\ \tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2 + C\sum_i\xi_i\quad\text{s.t.}\quad y_i(w^\top x_i + b) \ge 1 - \xi_i,\ \xi_i \ge 0.$$
A point with functional margin $1 - \xi_i$ costs $C\xi_i$ (CS229 section 6.7, an $\ell_1$ penalty on slack). Effects: small $C$ means wider margin, more support vectors, smoother boundary; large $C$ approaches the hard margin and is sensitive to outliers (a single outlier can swing the boundary). $C$ plays the role of $1/\lambda$ in regularisation. Tune it on a log grid by cross validation, jointly with $\gamma$ for RBF kernels.
say: C trades margin width against training errors. The soft margin SVM adds a slack variable per point that measures how far it violates the margin, and the objective is one half the squared norm of w plus C times the sum of slacks. Small C makes violations cheap, so I get a wide margin, many support vectors and a smoother, more biased boundary. Large C punishes every violation, giving a narrow margin that chases individual points and outliers, so variance goes up; at the extreme it's the hard margin SVM. So C acts like an inverse regularisation strength, and I tune it on a log scale with cross validation, together with gamma for an RBF kernel.
must_mention: small C wide margin more bias
large C narrow margin more variance
inverse regularisation, tune on log grid

followups.q: How well would a vanilla SVM work on overlapping data?
followups.a: A hard margin SVM has no solution; a soft margin SVM works if C is tuned.

followups.q: How does C relate to lambda?
followups.a: Roughly C equals one over lambda in the hinge loss plus L2 penalty form.

source.title: Chip Huyen, ML Interviews Book, classic ML questions

q: What is hinge loss, and how does an SVM compare with logistic regression?
plain: The soft margin SVM (support vector machine) is equivalent to minimising hinge loss plus a penalty on weight size. Hinge loss is zero for any point classified correctly with a comfortable margin. Hinge loss grows linearly as a point gets closer to, or crosses, the boundary. Log loss, used by logistic regression, never quite reaches zero, so every point always has some influence. That makes the SVM depend only on the points near the boundary. Logistic regression uses all points and gives probabilities. On most problems their accuracy is similar.
deep:
Eliminating slacks: $\min_{w,b}\ \tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2 + C\sum_i\max(0, 1 - y_if(x_i))$, $f(x) = w^\top x + b$.

| | SVM (hinge) | Logistic regression (log loss) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loss | $\max(0, 1 - yf)$ | $\log(1 + e^{-yf})$ |
| Beyond the margin | exactly zero | small but positive |
| Solution depends on | support vectors only | all points |
| Output | score (distance) | calibrated probability |
| Probabilities | need Platt scaling | native |
| Kernels | natural via the dual | possible but dense |
| Outliers | linear penalty | linear penalty asymptotically |

Both are convex surrogates of the 0/1 loss. The perceptron loss $\max(0, -yf)$ is hinge without the margin.
say: The SVM objective can be written as hinge loss, max of zero and one minus y times the score, plus an L2 penalty on w. Hinge loss is exactly zero once a point is correctly classified beyond the margin, so those points have no influence and the solution depends only on the support vectors. Log loss is a smooth version that never reaches zero, so every point keeps a little influence, and its output is a calibrated probability. In practice their accuracy is usually close. I'd pick logistic regression when I need probabilities or interpretability, and a kernel SVM for small to medium data with nonlinear boundaries, adding Platt scaling if I need probabilities.
must_mention: hinge loss max of zero and one minus y f
both convex surrogates of zero one loss

followups.q: What is Platt scaling?
followups.a: Fitting a sigmoid on SVM scores on held out data to turn them into probabilities.

followups.q: Which is more sensitive to outliers?
followups.a: Both grow linearly for badly misclassified points; the hard margin SVM is the fragile one.

q: Derive the SVM dual. What are support vectors in terms of the KKT conditions?
plain: To derive the SVM (support vector machine) dual, turn the constrained problem into a Lagrangian (a formula that folds the constraints in). The Lagrangian has one multiplier per training point. Then minimise over the weights. The optimal weight vector turns out to be a weighted sum of training points, with each point's weight equal to its multiplier times its label. Plugging that back in gives a dual problem that depends on the data only through dot products between pairs of points. That dependence on dot products is what makes kernels possible. Complementary slackness, one of the Karush Kuhn Tucker (KKT) conditions, says a multiplier can be nonzero only for points exactly on or inside the margin. Those points are the support vectors, often a small fraction of the data.
deep:
Lagrangian (hard margin): $\mathcal{L} = \tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2 - \sum_i\alpha_i[y_i(w^\top x_i + b) - 1]$, $\alpha_i \ge 0$.
$\nabla_w\mathcal{L} = 0 \Rightarrow w = \sum_i\alpha_iy_ix_i$; $\partial_b\mathcal{L} = 0 \Rightarrow \sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0$. Substituting:
$$\max_\alpha\ \sum_i\alpha_i - \tfrac12\sum_{i,j}y_iy_j\alpha_i\alpha_j\langle x_i, x_j\rangle\quad\text{s.t. } 0 \le \alpha_i \le C,\ \sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0$$
(the soft margin only adds the upper bound $C$; CS229 sections 6.5 to 6.7). Strong duality holds (convex, Slater).

KKT complementary slackness: $\alpha_i = 0 \Rightarrow y_if(x_i) \ge 1$; $0 < \alpha_i < C \Rightarrow y_if(x_i) = 1$ (on the margin); $\alpha_i = C \Rightarrow y_if(x_i) \le 1$ (violators). Prediction $f(x) = \sum_i\alpha_iy_i\langle x_i, x\rangle + b$ uses support vectors only. SMO optimises two $\alpha$ at a time because the equality constraint pins any single one. Verified: sklearn's largest $|\alpha_iy_i|$ equalled $C$ exactly.
say: I form the Lagrangian with a nonnegative multiplier alpha i per margin constraint, then set the derivatives with respect to w and b to zero. That gives w equals the sum of alpha i y i x i, and the constraint that the sum of alpha i y i is zero. Substituting back yields the dual: maximise the sum of alphas minus one half the double sum of alpha i alpha j y i y j times the inner product of x i and x j, with alphas between zero and C. The data appear only through inner products, which enables kernels. Complementary slackness says alpha i is nonzero only when the constraint is tight, so only points on or inside the margin, the support vectors, determine the solution.
must_mention: w equals sum of alpha y x
dual depends on inner products only

followups.q: Why does SMO update two multipliers at once?
followups.a: The equality constraint fixes any single alpha given the others, so at least two must move together.

followups.q: How is b recovered?
followups.a: From any support vector with alpha strictly between zero and C, where y times f of x equals one.

source.title: Stanford CS229 main notes, Spring 2026

q: What is the kernel trick?
plain: The kernel trick computes a dot product in a huge feature space without ever building that space. Some patterns that a straight line cannot separate become separable once you add combined features, such as squares and products of the original ones. Computing all those features explicitly can be enormous. But many algorithms, including the SVM (support vector machine), only ever need dot products between pairs of data points. A kernel function computes the dot product in the big feature space directly from the original inputs. For three inputs, the kernel (x dot z plus 1) squared equals the dot product of 13 explicit features. In a test, both ways gave 1.730612, while the kernel only needed one 3 dimensional dot product.
deep:
If an algorithm uses data only via $\langle x_i, x_j\rangle$, replace it with $K(x_i, x_j) = \langle\phi(x_i), \phi(x_j)\rangle$ to work in feature space without computing $\phi$ (CS229 chapter 5).

Example: $K(x, z) = (x^\top z + 1)^2 = \langle\phi(x), \phi(z)\rangle$ with $\phi(x) = (1, \sqrt2x_1, \dots, \sqrt2x_d, x_ix_j)$; for $(x^\top z + c)^k$ the space has $\binom{d+k}{k}$ dimensions but $K$ costs $O(d)$.

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x, z = rng.normal(size=3), rng.normal(size=3)
phi = lambda v: np.r_[1, np.sqrt(2) * v, np.outer(v, v).ravel()]
print(round((x @ z + 1) ** 2, 6), round(phi(x) @ phi(z), 6))  # 1.730612 1.730612
```

Applies to SVMs, kernel ridge, kernel PCA, the kernel perceptron, and LMS (CS229 section 5.3, where $\theta = \sum_i\beta_i\phi(x_i)$ and updates touch only $\beta$).
say: The kernel trick says: if an algorithm only touches the data through inner products, I can replace each inner product with a kernel function that equals an inner product in some high dimensional feature space, and never compute the features. For example, x dot z plus one, squared, equals the inner product of feature vectors containing all the pairwise products, thirteen features for three inputs, but costs one three dimensional dot product. In general a degree k polynomial kernel corresponds to order d to the k features at order d cost, and the RBF kernel corresponds to an infinite dimensional space. SVMs benefit because their dual and predictions depend only on inner products.
must_mention: kernel equals inner product of feature maps

followups.q: Which algorithms can be kernelised?
followups.a: Anything expressible through inner products: SVMs, ridge regression, PCA, the perceptron, kNN with kernel distances.

followups.q: Why can't lasso use the kernel trick?
followups.a: Its solution is not expressible as a function of inner products of features.

source.title: Stanford CS229 main notes, Spring 2026

q: What makes a function a valid kernel? How do you tune an RBF kernel SVM, and when should you avoid kernel SVMs?
plain: A function is a valid kernel if, for any set of points, the table of its pairwise values is symmetric and never produces negative variance. That property is called positive semidefinite. Then some feature space must exist in which the function is a dot product. The RBF (radial basis function) kernel scores similarity as a bell curve of distance and is always valid. The gamma setting of the RBF kernel controls how far each point's influence reaches. Large gamma gives a wiggly boundary around individual points, and small gamma gives a nearly straight one. Kernel SVMs (support vector machines) get slow and memory hungry past roughly a hundred thousand rows. Past that size, use a linear model or boosted trees (many small trees built one after another).
deep:
Mercer (CS229 section 5.4): $K$ is valid iff for every finite set the Gram matrix $K_{ij} = K(x_i, x_j)$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Proof of necessity: $z^\top Kz = \sum_k(\sum_iz_i\phi_k(x_i))^2 \ge 0$. Verified: an RBF Gram matrix on 50 points had smallest eigenvalue $3.2 \times 10^{-2}$. Valid kernels are closed under sums, positive scaling, products and limits.

RBF: $K(x, z) = \exp(-\gamma\lVert x - z\rVert^2)$, $\gamma = 1/(2\sigma^2)$. Large $\gamma$: local influence, high variance; small $\gamma$: near linear. Tune $(C, \gamma)$ jointly on a log grid by CV. Scale features first; distances drive everything.

Scaling: training between $O(n^2)$ and $O(n^3)$; memory for the kernel matrix; prediction cost proportional to the number of support vectors. Alternatives at scale: `LinearSVC`, random Fourier features (`RBFSampler`), Nystroem approximation, gradient boosting.
say: A kernel is valid exactly when every Gram matrix it produces is symmetric positive semidefinite; that's Mercer's theorem, and it guarantees some feature map exists. Sums, products and positive multiples of valid kernels stay valid. For the RBF kernel, exp of minus gamma times squared distance, gamma sets the reach of each point: large gamma makes influence very local and the boundary wiggly, small gamma makes it nearly linear. I tune C and gamma together on a log grid with cross validation, after scaling features. I'd avoid kernel SVMs beyond roughly a hundred thousand rows, since training scales between quadratically and cubically, and use a linear SVM, random features, or boosted trees instead.

followups.q: Is cosine similarity a valid kernel?
followups.a: Yes, it is the linear kernel on normalised vectors.

followups.q: Is feature scaling necessary for kernel methods?
followups.a: Yes; unscaled features dominate the distances and inner products.

source.title: Stanford CS229 main notes, Spring 2026

q: How is a decision tree trained?
plain: A decision tree is learned top down, one question at a time. At the root, the tree tries every feature and every possible threshold, such as income above 50,000. The tree picks the split that makes the two resulting groups as pure (mostly one class) as possible. The tree then repeats the same search inside each group, and keeps going until the groups are pure, too small, or a depth limit is hit. Each final group, called a leaf, predicts its majority class or average value. The search is greedy: it never revisits an earlier split, so the tree is good but not guaranteed best.
deep:
CART (sklearn's algorithm): recursive binary splitting. At node $m$ with data $Q_m$, choose feature $j$ and threshold $t$ minimising
$$\frac{n_L}{n_m}H(Q_L) + \frac{n_R}{n_m}H(Q_R),$$
with impurity $H$ = Gini or entropy (classification) or MSE (regression). Recurse until a stopping rule (`max_depth`, `min_samples_split`, `min_samples_leaf`, `min_impurity_decrease`) or purity. Leaves predict the majority class (with class proportions as probabilities) or the mean.

Greedy top down search is used because finding the optimal tree is NP hard. Cost roughly $O(d\,n\log n)$ per level with sorting.
say: A decision tree is grown greedily from the top. At each node I consider every feature and candidate threshold, compute how much the split reduces impurity, measured by Gini or entropy for classification or variance for regression, weighted by the sizes of the two children, and take the best split. Then I recurse into each child until a stopping rule kicks in: maximum depth, minimum samples per leaf, or no worthwhile impurity decrease. Leaves predict the majority class or the mean. It's greedy because finding the optimal tree is NP hard, so a split that looks mediocre now but enables great splits later can be missed.
must_mention: choose split by weighted impurity decrease

followups.q: What are the main parameters of a decision tree?
followups.a: max_depth, min_samples_split, min_samples_leaf, max_features, criterion, and ccp_alpha for pruning.

followups.q: What are the benefits of a single tree?
followups.a: Readable rules, no scaling needed, fast, handles interactions and mixed feature types.

source.title: Alexey Grigorev, data science interview theory questions

q: Compute the Gini impurity, entropy and information gain for a split.
plain: Gini impurity is the chance that two randomly drawn examples from a group have different labels. Entropy measures how many bits of uncertainty the group holds. Take a group of 10 buyers and 10 non buyers: Gini is 0.5 and entropy is 1 bit, the most mixed possible. Now split it into 8 buyers with 2 non buyers, and 2 buyers with 8 non buyers. Each child then has Gini 0.32 and entropy 0.72 bits. Information gain is the parent's impurity minus the size weighted average of the children's. Here information gain is 1 minus 0.72, about 0.28 bits.
deep:
For class proportions $p_k$: Gini $= 1 - \sum_kp_k^2$, entropy $= -\sum_kp_k\log_2p_k$.

Parent $(0.5, 0.5)$: Gini $1 - 0.25 - 0.25 = 0.5$; entropy $1$.
Children $(0.8, 0.2)$ and $(0.2, 0.8)$, each half the data: Gini $1 - 0.64 - 0.04 = 0.32$; entropy $-0.8\log_20.8 - 0.2\log_20.2 = 0.7219$.
Weighted children: Gini 0.32, entropy 0.7219. Gain: Gini decrease 0.18; information gain $1 - 0.7219 = 0.2781$ bits (verified numerically).

Regression trees use the decrease in variance (MSE) the same way.
say: Gini is one minus the sum of squared class proportions, and entropy is minus the sum of p log base two of p. Take a parent with ten positives and ten negatives: Gini is 0.5 and entropy is one bit. Split it into children of eight two and two eight. Each child has Gini one minus 0.64 minus 0.04, which is 0.32, and entropy of about 0.72 bits. Because the children are equal sized, the weighted impurity is the same, so the Gini decreases by 0.18 and the information gain is one minus 0.72, about 0.28 bits. The tree would compare that gain against every other candidate split.
must_mention: Gini one minus sum of squared proportions
entropy minus sum p log p
gain is parent minus weighted children

followups.q: What is the maximum Gini for two classes?
followups.a: 0.5, at a fifty fifty split; entropy's maximum is one bit.

followups.q: How do regression trees measure impurity?
followups.a: Variance or MSE of the target within the node.

q: Gini impurity, entropy or misclassification rate: which should a tree use to choose splits?
plain: A tree should use Gini or entropy to choose splits, not misclassification rate. Gini and entropy behave almost identically and pick the same split in the vast majority of cases. Gini is slightly faster because it needs no logarithms. Misclassification rate, the fraction of the minority class, is a poor choice for growing trees. Misclassification rate often does not change even when a split clearly makes the groups purer. For example, splitting 40 versus 60 into 30 versus 50 and 10 versus 10 leaves the error count unchanged, while Gini and entropy both register an improvement. Misclassification rate is still reasonable for judging pruning.
deep:
Two class impurities as functions of $p$: Gini $2p(1 - p)$, entropy $-p\log p - (1 - p)\log(1 - p)$, misclassification $\min(p, 1 - p)$. Gini and entropy are strictly concave, so any split that changes class proportions strictly decreases weighted impurity; misclassification is piecewise linear, so many splits give zero decrease and growth stalls.

Entropy based gain is biased toward attributes with many values (each value can isolate few examples); C4.5 corrects with gain ratio, gain divided by split information. sklearn supports `criterion="gini"`, `"entropy"` and `"log_loss"`; differences in accuracy are usually negligible.
say: In practice Gini and entropy almost always choose the same split, and Gini is a bit cheaper since there's no log. The one to avoid for growing trees is misclassification rate: it's piecewise linear in the class proportion, so many splits that genuinely purify the children don't change the error count at all, and the tree stops growing too early. Gini and entropy are strictly concave, so any split that changes the class proportions shows a strict improvement. One more nuance: entropy based information gain favours features with many distinct values, which is why C4.5 uses gain ratio. For pruning or evaluating a finished tree, misclassification rate is fine.
must_mention: Gini and entropy nearly always agree
gain ratio corrects many valued bias

followups.q: Why does concavity matter?
followups.a: Strictly concave impurity guarantees the weighted children's impurity is below the parent's whenever proportions change.

followups.q: Which features does impurity based gain favour?
followups.a: Those with many distinct values, such as IDs, because they offer many candidate splits.

q: How does a tree find the best split for numeric and for categorical features?
plain: For a numeric feature, sort the values once, then slide a threshold between each pair of neighbouring values. Update the class counts on each side as you go, and keep the threshold with the biggest impurity drop. With 1,000 distinct ages that is 999 candidate thresholds, but each is checked cheaply. For a categorical feature with many levels, trying every way to split the levels into two groups explodes quickly. A shortcut for yes or no targets is to sort the categories by their rate of positives and treat them as ordered. That shortcut finds the best split without trying them all.
deep:
Numeric: sort once ($O(n\log n)$), scan $n - 1$ thresholds with running sufficient statistics, $O(n)$ per feature per node after sorting. Histogram methods (LightGBM, `HistGradientBoosting`) bin features into about 255 bins, making the scan $O(\text{bins})$.

Categorical with $k$ levels: $2^{k-1} - 1$ binary partitions. For binary targets (and squared error regression), ordering levels by mean target and splitting as if ordinal is optimal (Breiman et al.'s CART result). Plain sklearn trees require numeric encoding (one hot or ordinal); `HistGradientBoosting`, LightGBM and CatBoost handle categoricals natively. Target based encodings must be computed out of fold to avoid leakage. XGBoost and LightGBM also learn a default direction for missing values at each split.
say: For a numeric feature I sort the values once and scan all thresholds between consecutive distinct values, updating class counts incrementally, so each feature costs about n log n per node, or much less with histograms, which bin each feature into a couple of hundred buckets as LightGBM does. For categorical features, trying every subset of k categories is exponential. For a binary target there's a classic shortcut: sort the categories by their positive rate and treat them as ordered, which provably finds the best binary partition. In sklearn's plain trees I have to encode categoricals myself, while histogram gradient boosting, LightGBM and CatBoost handle them natively.

followups.q: How do we handle categorical variables in decision trees?
followups.a: One hot or ordinal encoding for sklearn trees, native support in histogram boosting libraries, or target encoding computed out of fold.

followups.q: Why is one hot encoding bad for high cardinality features in trees?
followups.a: Each dummy is a weak, rarely split feature; the tree needs many splits to group levels.

source.title: Alexey Grigorev, data science interview theory questions

q: How do you stop a decision tree from overfitting? Explain pre pruning and cost complexity pruning.
plain: A tree grown until every leaf is pure memorises the training data, including its noise. Pre pruning stops growth early using limits such as a maximum depth or a minimum number of examples per leaf. Post pruning grows the full tree and then cuts back branches whose accuracy gain does not justify their size. Cost complexity pruning (a kind of post pruning) uses a penalty per leaf, with the penalty chosen by cross validation. In a test on a medical dataset, pruning cut a tree from 16 leaves to 9. That pruning raised test accuracy from 0.881 to 0.916.
deep:
Pre pruning: `max_depth`, `min_samples_leaf`, `min_samples_split`, `max_leaf_nodes`, `min_impurity_decrease`. Risk: stopping before a weak split that would enable strong later splits (horizon effect).

Cost complexity (weakest link) pruning: minimise $R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha|T|$, where $R(T)$ is training error or impurity and $|T|$ the number of leaves. Increasing $\alpha$ yields a nested sequence of subtrees; pick $\alpha$ by CV (sklearn `cost_complexity_pruning_path`, `ccp_alpha`).

```python
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)
path = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).cost_complexity_pruning_path(X_tr, y_tr)
best = max(path.ccp_alphas[:-1], key=lambda a: cross_val_score(
    DecisionTreeClassifier(ccp_alpha=a, random_state=0), X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean())
t = DecisionTreeClassifier(ccp_alpha=best, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(t.get_n_leaves(), round(t.score(X_te, y_te), 3))  # 9 0.916 (full tree: 16 leaves, 0.881)
```
say: An unconstrained tree keeps splitting until leaves are pure, which memorises noise. Pre pruning limits growth up front with max depth, minimum samples per leaf, or a minimum impurity decrease; it's cheap but can stop before a weak split that would have enabled strong ones. Post pruning grows the full tree, then removes subtrees using cost complexity: minimise training error plus alpha times the number of leaves, which gives a nested sequence of subtrees, and I pick alpha by cross validation. On the breast cancer dataset, pruning took a tree from sixteen leaves to nine and raised test accuracy from 0.88 to 0.92. In practice, ensembles often make pruning less important.
must_mention: pre pruning with depth and leaf limits
cost complexity adds alpha per leaf

followups.q: How do you select the depth of trees in a random forest?
followups.a: Usually grow deep and control variance by averaging; tune min_samples_leaf if needed.

followups.q: What is the horizon effect?
followups.a: Early stopping can miss a useful split hidden behind a split that alone looks unhelpful.

source.title: Alexey Grigorev, data science interview theory questions

q: What are the strengths and failure modes of a single decision tree?
plain: Trees are easy to read as if then rules. Trees need no feature scaling and handle a mix of numeric and categorical inputs. Trees capture interactions, such as a discount mattering only for new customers. Their big weakness is instability. A small change in the training data can change the top split and therefore the whole tree, so variance is high. Tree boundaries are made of axis aligned steps, so a diagonal pattern needs many splits. A regression tree cannot predict beyond the range it saw. Trained on prices up to 500, a regression tree will never predict 600 even if the trend clearly continues.
deep:
Strengths: invariant to monotone transforms of features; no scaling; handles interactions and nonlinearity; fast prediction $O(\text{depth})$; readable when shallow; can handle missing values with surrogate splits or learned default directions.

Failure modes:
- High variance: small data changes flip early splits; fixed by bagging and random forests.
- Axis aligned staircase boundaries for oblique structure.
- No extrapolation: predictions are leaf means, bounded by the training range of $y$; critical for trending time series (difference or detrend first).
- Greedy, not globally optimal.
- Impurity importance biased toward high cardinality features.
- Probability estimates from small leaves are coarse and poorly calibrated.
say: The strengths are interpretability when shallow, no need for scaling, robustness to monotone transformations, natural handling of mixed feature types and interactions, and fast prediction. The weaknesses: high variance, since a small change in the data can flip the root split and produce a completely different tree; staircase boundaries that need many splits to approximate a diagonal; greedy construction that isn't globally optimal; and no extrapolation, because a regression tree predicts leaf averages, so it can never output a value beyond what it saw in training. That last one matters a lot for trending time series. Bagging and boosting exist largely to fix the variance problem.

followups.q: What are the problems with using trees for time series?
followups.a: They cannot extrapolate trends, so difference or detrend first, and lag features must be built from past values only.

followups.q: How can we know which features are important to a tree?
followups.a: Impurity based importance, which is biased, or permutation importance on held out data.

source.title: Alexey Grigorev, data science interview theory questions

q: What is bagging, and why does it reduce variance?
plain: Bagging, short for bootstrap aggregating, trains many copies of a model and averages their predictions (or takes a vote). Each copy trains on a different random resample of the training data, drawn with replacement. Each individual deep tree is jumpy and overfits its sample. But the trees' mistakes partly cancel when averaged, like a crowd's average guess beating most individuals. Bagging helps high variance models such as deep trees a lot. Bagging helps stable models such as linear regression very little. Bagging barely changes bias, because each copy is the same kind of model.
deep:
Algorithm: for $b = 1..B$, draw a bootstrap sample of size $n$ with replacement, fit $\hat f_b$; predict $\hat f_{\text{bag}}(x) = \frac1B\sum_b\hat f_b(x)$ (or majority vote, or averaged probabilities).

Why it works: averaging reduces the variance term; if the $\hat f_b$ were independent with variance $\sigma^2$, the average would have variance $\sigma^2/B$. They are correlated (same training set), which limits the gain. Bias is roughly unchanged. Most effective for unstable, low bias learners (deep trees, kNN with small $k$ is less helped because resampling changes it little). Each bootstrap sample omits about 36.8 percent of rows, which gives free out of bag validation.
say: Bagging means drawing many bootstrap samples, sampling n rows with replacement, fitting the same model to each, and averaging the predictions or taking a vote. It reduces variance because each model overfits its own sample in a different way, and averaging cancels part of that noise; if the models were independent, the variance would fall by a factor of B. Bias stays about the same, since every member is the same kind of model. So bagging is most useful for unstable, low bias learners like deep decision trees, and nearly useless for stable ones like linear regression. A side benefit is that each sample leaves out about a third of the rows, which gives a free validation estimate.
must_mention: best for unstable learners like deep trees

followups.q: Why doesn't bagging help linear regression much?
followups.a: Linear regression is stable: resampled fits barely differ, so there is little variance to average away.

followups.q: How are bagged trees used in deep learning analogues?
followups.a: Ensembles of independently trained networks and dropout both average over many slightly different models.

source.title: Chip Huyen, ML Interviews Book, classic ML questions

q: Derive the variance of an average of B correlated predictors. What does it imply for ensembles?
plain: Suppose each of B predictors has variance sigma squared, and every pair has correlation rho. The variance of their average is rho times sigma squared, plus the remaining part divided by B. The second piece shrinks as you add predictors. The first piece does not shrink: it is a floor set by how correlated the predictors are. With 50 trees whose errors are 30 percent correlated, the average has variance 0.314 of a single tree's. No number of extra trees can push the variance below 0.30. So making trees less alike matters more than making many of them.
deep:
$$\mathrm{Var}\Big(\frac1B\sum_b X_b\Big) = \frac1{B^2}\Big(\sum_b\mathrm{Var}X_b + \sum_{b \ne b'}\mathrm{Cov}(X_b, X_{b'})\Big) = \frac{1}{B^2}\big(B\sigma^2 + B(B - 1)\rho\sigma^2\big) = \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1 - \rho}{B}\sigma^2.$$
As $B \to \infty$, variance $\to \rho\sigma^2$. Verified: with $\rho = 0.3$, $B = 50$, simulation gave 0.3154 against the formula's 0.314.

Implications: past a few hundred trees, only lower $\rho$ helps; random forests lower $\rho$ by subsampling features at each split, at the cost of slightly weaker (higher variance, higher bias) individual trees.
say: Write the variance of the mean as one over B squared times the sum of all variances and covariances. There are B variance terms of sigma squared and B times B minus one covariance terms of rho sigma squared. Dividing through gives rho sigma squared plus one minus rho over B times sigma squared. The second term vanishes as B grows, but the first is a floor that only depends on the correlation between members. With rho of 0.3 and fifty members, a simulation matched the formula at about 0.31. The implication is that beyond a few hundred trees, adding more does little; what helps is making the trees less correlated, which is exactly what random forests do.
must_mention: rho sigma squared plus one minus rho over B sigma squared

followups.q: What is the variance with independent members?
followups.a: sigma squared over B, the rho equals zero case.

followups.q: How do random forests reduce rho?
followups.a: Each split considers a random subset of features, so trees cannot all use the same dominant splits.

q: What is a random forest, and why does it choose a random subset of features at each split?
plain: A random forest is bagging of decision trees with one extra twist. At every split, each tree may only choose among a random handful of features rather than all of them. Without this twist, if one feature is very strong, almost every tree would split on it first. The trees would then look alike, so their errors would be correlated and averaging would help less. Forcing variety makes the trees disagree more, which makes the average more accurate. In one test, plain bagged trees reached 0.909 accuracy and the random forest reached 0.920 on the same data.
deep:
Random forest = bootstrap samples plus random feature subsampling per split (`max_features`), usually with deep, unpruned trees (low bias, variance averaged away).

Effect: lowers inter tree correlation $\rho$ in $\rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1 - \rho}{B}\sigma^2$, at the cost of slightly weaker trees. Typical settings: $\sqrt{d}$ features for classification; a larger fraction for regression (classic recommendation $d/3$; recent sklearn regressor defaults use all features, so tune it). Smaller `max_features` decorrelates more; too small and trees become too weak.

Verified: on a 20 feature synthetic task, `max_features=1.0` (bagging) gave test accuracy 0.909 and `"sqrt"` gave 0.920.
say: A random forest is an ensemble of deep decision trees, each trained on a bootstrap sample, where every split considers only a random subset of the features, typically the square root of the feature count for classification. The feature subsampling is the important part. If one feature dominates, bagged trees would all split on it at the top and end up highly correlated, and averaging correlated trees has a variance floor. Restricting the candidates at each split forces trees to differ, lowering that correlation. Each tree gets a bit weaker, but the ensemble gets better. In a quick test, bagging alone scored 0.909 and the forest 0.920. max_features is the main knob for this trade off.
must_mention: bootstrap plus random features per split
max_features trades tree strength for diversity

followups.q: Why do we need randomisation in random forests?
followups.a: To decorrelate the trees so averaging reduces variance further.

followups.q: What are the main parameters?
followups.a: n_estimators, max_features, max_depth or min_samples_leaf, and bootstrap.

source.title: Alexey Grigorev, data science interview theory questions

q: What is Breiman's generalisation bound for random forests in terms of strength and correlation?
plain: Breiman showed that a forest's error is bounded by the average correlation between trees times a term that depends on how strong each tree is. Strength means how confidently the trees vote for the right class on average. Strong trees lower the bound, and correlated trees raise it. So the goal is trees that are individually good but disagree with each other. The bound itself is loose and not used for numbers in practice. But the bound gives the right intuition for tuning how many features each split may consider.
deep:
Margin function $mr(X, Y) = P_\Theta(h(X, \Theta) = Y) - \max_{j \ne Y}P_\Theta(h(X, \Theta) = j)$; strength $s = \mathbb{E}_{X,Y}\,mr(X, Y)$; $\bar\rho$ the mean correlation of the raw margin functions between trees. Breiman (2001), Theorem 2.3:
$$PE^* \le \frac{\bar\rho\,(1 - s^2)}{s^2}.$$
The ratio $c/s^2 = \bar\rho/s^2$ is the guide: smaller is better. It also shows that the generalisation error converges almost surely as trees are added, so more trees do not overfit. Breiman estimated strength and correlation out of bag to choose the number of features per split.
say: In the 2001 paper, Breiman bounds the forest's generalisation error by the mean correlation between trees times one minus strength squared, over strength squared, where strength is the expected margin, roughly how much more often the trees vote for the right class than the best wrong one. The bound is loose, but it captures the design principle: you want strong individual trees and low correlation between them, and those pull against each other through the number of features considered at each split. He used out of bag estimates of strength and correlation to tune that. The same paper shows the forest's error converges as trees are added, which is why more trees don't overfit.
must_mention: error bounded by correlation times a strength term
bound is loose but guides max_features
error converges as trees are added

followups.q: What is the c over s squared ratio?
followups.a: Mean correlation divided by squared strength; Breiman's guide, smaller is better.

followups.q: Does adding trees overfit?
followups.a: No; the generalisation error converges almost surely to a limit.

source.title: Breiman (2001), Random Forests

q: What is out of bag error, and why is about 37 percent of the data out of bag for each tree?
plain: Out of bag error scores every row using only the trees that never saw it. Each tree in a random forest trains on a bootstrap sample, which by chance leaves out some rows. Out of bag error gives a validation estimate for free, without a separate holdout set. A given row is missed by one draw with probability 1 minus 1 over n. A row is missed by all n draws with probability about 1 over e, roughly 0.368. That is why about 37 percent of the data is out of bag for each tree. In one test, the out of bag accuracy was 0.906 while the true test accuracy was 0.920. The out of bag estimate was close and slightly pessimistic.
deep:
$P(\text{row } i \notin \text{bootstrap}) = (1 - 1/n)^n \to e^{-1} \approx 0.368$ (verified: 0.3677 at $n = 1000$).

OOB prediction for row $i$: aggregate only trees whose bootstrap sample excluded $i$ (about $0.37B$ trees). OOB error: error of these predictions over the training set. Breiman reports it is about as accurate as a test set of the training set's size, and slightly pessimistic early on because each row is scored by only about a third of the trees, so run past the point where it stabilises.

```python
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=3000, n_features=20, n_informative=6, random_state=0)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, oob_score=True, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(round(rf.oob_score_, 3), round(rf.score(X_te, y_te), 3))  # 0.906 0.92
```

Caveat: OOB is not valid for grouped or time ordered data, for the same reasons random CV is not.
say: Each tree trains on a bootstrap sample, and any given row is left out of it with probability one minus one over n, raised to the n, which tends to one over e, about 37 percent. So for every row there are roughly a third of the trees that never saw it, and I can score the row using only those. Averaged over the training set, that's the out of bag error, essentially free cross validation. Breiman found it about as accurate as a test set of the same size, slightly pessimistic since each row gets fewer trees. In a quick test the OOB accuracy was 0.906 against 0.920 on the test set. It's not valid with grouped or time ordered data.
must_mention: one minus one over n to the n
tends to one over e, about 0.368
score rows with trees that did not see them
invalid for grouped or temporal data

followups.q: How do you know how many trees you need?
followups.a: Plot OOB error against the number of trees and stop when it flattens.

followups.q: Why is OOB slightly pessimistic?
followups.a: Each row is scored by only about a third of the forest, a smaller ensemble than the full one.

source.title: Breiman (2001), Random Forests

q: What practical behaviours of random forests do interviewers ask about: more trees, parallelism, correlated features, and extremely randomised trees?
plain: Adding more trees never makes a random forest overfit in the sense of rising test error. The error just levels off, so the number of trees is limited by time, not accuracy. Trees are built independently, so training splits across CPU (central processing unit) cores trivially. When two features carry the same information, the forest splits credit between them. So each of those features looks less important than it really is. Extremely randomised trees go further and pick split thresholds at random instead of searching for the best. Extremely randomised trees train faster and often generalise as well.
deep:
- **Number of trees:** error converges (Breiman); choose $B$ where OOB error flattens; cost is linear in $B$.
- **Parallelism:** embarrassingly parallel over trees (`n_jobs=-1`); prediction too.
- **Depth:** usually grow deep; tune `min_samples_leaf` if leaves are noisy; deep trees cost memory.
- **Correlated features:** importance (MDI or permutation) is shared or masked; cluster correlated features before interpreting.
- **Extra trees** (`ExtraTreesClassifier`): random thresholds per candidate feature, choose the best of those; lower variance, slightly higher bias, faster. Answers the interview question "what if we randomly select a few splits and pick the best?": yes, it works.
- **Weaknesses:** large models, slow prediction for many deep trees, no extrapolation, probabilities pulled away from 0 and 1.
say: First, more trees don't overfit: test error converges, so I add trees until the out of bag error flattens and stop for cost reasons. Second, trees are independent, so training and prediction parallelise trivially across cores. Third, with correlated features the forest splits credit between them, so both look less important than they are, which matters when interpreting importances. Fourth, extremely randomised trees replace the threshold search with random thresholds and pick the best among those; that adds a bit of bias but cuts variance and training time, so yes, randomly choosing a few splits works. The downsides are big models, slowish prediction with many deep trees, and no extrapolation.
must_mention: more trees converge, do not overfit

followups.q: What are the potential problems with many large trees?
followups.a: Memory use and slow prediction latency; consider fewer trees, shallower trees, or distillation.

followups.q: Is it easy to parallelise random forest training?
followups.a: Yes, each tree is independent; split them across workers.

source.title: Alexey Grigorev, data science interview theory questions

q: What are the fundamental differences between bagging and boosting?
plain: Bagging trains many models independently on resampled data and averages them, which mainly cuts variance. Bagging works best with strong, overfitting models like deep trees. Boosting trains models one after another, each focusing on the mistakes of the ensemble so far, and adds them up. Boosting mainly cuts bias, and it works best with weak models like shallow trees. Think of bagging as a committee voting independently. Think of boosting as a relay team where each runner starts where the last one stumbled. Bagging parallelises easily. Boosting is sequential and can overfit if you keep adding models.
deep:
| | Bagging / random forest | Boosting (AdaBoost, gradient boosting) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Training | parallel, independent | sequential, each depends on the previous |
| Base learner | strong, low bias, high variance (deep trees) | weak, high bias (stumps, shallow trees) |
| Reduces | variance | bias first, variance via shrinkage and subsampling |
| Combination | equal weight average or vote | weighted sum |
| More members | converges, does not overfit | overfits without early stopping |
| Noise sensitivity | low | higher (AdaBoost especially) |

In deep learning, ensembling independent networks is bagging like, and residual stacking of weak learners appears in boosting style methods.
say: Bagging fits many models independently on bootstrap samples and averages them, so it reduces variance and wants strong, low bias base learners like deep trees. Boosting fits models sequentially, each one trained to fix what the current ensemble gets wrong, either by reweighting examples as in AdaBoost or by fitting residuals as in gradient boosting, so it reduces bias and uses weak learners like shallow trees. Bagging parallelises trivially and adding members never hurts; boosting is inherently sequential across trees and will overfit if I keep adding them without early stopping. Boosting usually wins on accuracy for tabular data, while bagging is more forgiving and harder to break.

followups.q: How are they used in deep learning?
followups.a: Ensembles of independently trained networks are bagging like; snapshot ensembles and some residual schemes resemble boosting.

followups.q: Which is more sensitive to label noise?
followups.a: Boosting, because it keeps upweighting hard examples, which include mislabelled ones.

source.title: Chip Huyen, ML Interviews Book, classic ML questions

q: How does AdaBoost work? Give the weight update and the formula for each learner's vote.
plain: AdaBoost (adaptive boosting) starts with every training example weighted equally. Each round, AdaBoost fits a weak classifier, such as a one split tree, to the weighted data. AdaBoost then measures the classifier's weighted error, and gives it a vote that is larger the more accurate it is. AdaBoost then increases the weights of the examples the classifier got wrong, so the next weak learner focuses on them. A learner with 10 percent error gets a vote of 1.10, and one with 30 percent gets 0.42. A learner at 50 percent error, no better than a coin, gets a vote of 0. AdaBoost's exponential style penalty makes it sensitive to mislabelled examples.
deep:
Labels $y_i \in \{-1, +1\}$, weights $w_i = 1/n$. For $m = 1..M$:
1. Fit $h_m$ to minimise weighted error $\epsilon_m = \sum_iw_i\mathbb{1}\{h_m(x_i) \ne y_i\}$.
2. $\alpha_m = \tfrac12\ln\frac{1 - \epsilon_m}{\epsilon_m}$ (verified: 1.099, 0.424, 0 for $\epsilon$ = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5).
3. $w_i \leftarrow w_i\exp(-\alpha_my_ih_m(x_i))$, then normalise.
Predict $\mathrm{sign}\big(\sum_m\alpha_mh_m(x)\big)$.

Interpretation: forward stagewise additive modelling under exponential loss $L = e^{-yF(x)}$; the $\alpha_m$ formula is the exact line search minimiser. Exponential loss grows fast on badly misclassified points, so label noise and outliers get huge weights, which is AdaBoost's main weakness; log loss (as in gradient boosting) grows only linearly.
say: AdaBoost keeps a weight on every training example, starting uniform. Each round I fit a weak learner, typically a decision stump, to the weighted data and compute its weighted error epsilon. Its vote is one half log of one minus epsilon over epsilon, so ten percent error earns about 1.1, thirty percent about 0.42, and fifty percent, coin flipping, earns zero. Then I multiply each example's weight by e to the minus alpha y h, which increases weights on misclassified points, and renormalise. The final prediction is the sign of the weighted vote. AdaBoost is forward stagewise fitting of exponential loss, which explains its sensitivity to label noise: misclassified points get exponentially growing weight.
must_mention: alpha one half log of one minus error over error

followups.q: What happens if a weak learner has error above 0.5?
followups.a: Its alpha turns negative, effectively flipping it; in practice the learner is discarded or the round stops.

followups.q: Why is AdaBoost sensitive to outliers?
followups.a: Exponential loss keeps multiplying the weight of a persistently misclassified point.

q: What is gradient boosting, and why is it described as gradient descent in function space?
plain: Gradient boosting builds a model as a sum of small trees, added one at a time. Each new tree is trained to predict the current errors of the ensemble, then a fraction of its prediction is added. For squared error, the errors the tree fits are literally the residuals. If the ensemble predicts 4 for a house worth 5, the next tree aims to output 1 there. More generally, each tree fits the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions. So each tree is one downhill step, taken on the predictions themselves rather than on a fixed set of weights. That is why gradient boosting is described as gradient descent in function space.
deep:
Treat the vector of predictions $F = (F(x_1), \dots, F(x_n))$ as the parameter. Friedman's algorithm:
1. $F_0 = \arg\min_c\sum_iL(y_i, c)$.
2. For $m = 1..M$: pseudo residuals $r_{im} = -\frac{\partial L(y_i, F)}{\partial F}\big|_{F = F_{m-1}(x_i)}$; fit a regression tree $h_m$ to $\{(x_i, r_{im})\}$; optionally re-solve each leaf value by line search on $L$; update $F_m = F_{m-1} + \nu h_m$.

Gradient descent would move each $F(x_i)$ directly along $r_{im}$, but that cannot generalise to new $x$; fitting a tree projects the gradient onto functions a tree can represent, which do generalise. Any differentiable loss works (squared, absolute, Huber, log loss, quantile, ranking losses).
say: Gradient boosting is an additive model of shallow trees built stage by stage. At each stage I compute, for every training row, the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current prediction, the pseudo residual, fit a small regression tree to those values, and add a shrunken copy of that tree to the model. For squared error the pseudo residual is just the ordinary residual, so each tree literally fits what's left over. It's gradient descent in function space because the thing being optimised is the prediction function itself: each tree is a step along the negative gradient, projected onto what a tree can represent, so the step generalises to new inputs. Any differentiable loss plugs in.
must_mention: pseudo residuals equal residuals for squared loss

followups.q: What is gradient boosting good for?
followups.a: Tabular data with mixed feature types and nonlinear interactions; it is the default winner on such data.

followups.q: Why fit a tree instead of moving predictions directly?
followups.a: Moving training predictions directly would not define predictions for new inputs; a tree generalises the step.

source.title: Chip Huyen, ML Interviews Book, classic ML questions

q: What are the pseudo residuals for squared error, absolute error and log loss in gradient boosting?
plain: The pseudo residual is what each new tree is asked to predict: the direction that would most reduce the loss at each training point. For squared error, the pseudo residual is the plain residual, actual minus predicted. So a prediction of 4 for a true value of 5 gives 1. For absolute error, the pseudo residual is just the sign of the residual, plus or minus 1. That makes the method resistant to outliers. For log loss in classification, the pseudo residual is the label minus the predicted probability. So a positive example predicted at 0.3 gives 0.7.
deep:
$r_i = -\partial L(y_i, F)/\partial F$ at $F = F_{m-1}(x_i)$:
| Loss | $L(y, F)$ | Pseudo residual |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Squared | $\tfrac12(y - F)^2$ | $y - F$ |
| Absolute | $\lvert y - F\rvert$ | $\mathrm{sign}(y - F)$ |
| Huber ($\delta$) | quadratic inside, linear outside | $y - F$ clipped to $\pm\delta$ |
| Log loss, $F$ = log odds | $-[y\log p + (1 - y)\log(1 - p)]$, $p = \sigma(F)$ | $y - p$ |
| Quantile $\tau$ | pinball | $\tau - \mathbb{1}\{y < F\}$ |

Leaf values are then set by a line search (or one Newton step, $\sum r_i/\sum p_i(1 - p_i)$ for log loss) rather than the tree's raw mean. XGBoost generalises this with gradients $g_i$ and Hessians $h_i$.
say: The pseudo residual is the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current prediction at each row. For half squared error that's y minus F, the ordinary residual. For absolute error it's the sign of y minus F, so every point pushes with the same strength, which makes the model resistant to outliers and pushes toward the conditional median. For log loss, with F as the log odds, it's y minus the predicted probability, so a positive example predicted at 0.3 contributes 0.7. Huber clips the residual at a threshold, and quantile loss gives tau minus an indicator. After fitting the tree to these, leaf values are usually refit with a line search or a Newton step.
must_mention: log loss gives y minus p
leaf values refit by line search or Newton step

followups.q: Which loss would you use for a skewed target with outliers?
followups.a: Absolute or Huber loss, or quantile loss for a chosen quantile.

followups.q: Why refit leaf values?
followups.a: The tree fits the gradient by least squares, which is not the loss's own optimal step for non squared losses.

q: Implement gradient boosting for squared error from scratch.
plain: Gradient boosting for squared error starts every prediction at the average target value. Then you repeat three steps. First, compute the residuals, which are actual minus current prediction. Second, fit a small regression tree to those residuals. Third, add the tree's predictions times a small learning rate, such as 0.1, to the current predictions. After 200 rounds with depth 2 trees on a noisy sine wave, this ten line loop reached a training error of 0.0203. That matched scikit-learn's GradientBoostingRegressor with the same settings exactly. The learning rate keeps each step small, which generalises better.
deep:
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(0, 1, (300, 1))
y = np.sin(2 * np.pi * X[:, 0]) + rng.normal(scale=0.2, size=300)

F = np.full(300, y.mean())                  # F_0 minimises squared loss
nu = 0.1                                    # shrinkage
trees = []
for m in range(200):
    residual = y - F                        # negative gradient of 0.5 * (y - F)^2
    tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=2).fit(X, residual)
    F += nu * tree.predict(X)
    trees.append(tree)
predict = lambda Xn: y.mean() + nu * sum(t.predict(Xn) for t in trees)
gb = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=2).fit(X, y)
print(round(np.mean((y - F) ** 2), 4), round(np.mean((y - gb.predict(X)) ** 2), 4))  # 0.0203 0.0203
```

Extensions: other losses change only the residual line (and leaf values); add row subsampling per tree; stop early on a validation set; keep the trees to predict on new data.
say: I initialise every prediction to the mean of y, because that's the constant minimising squared error. Then for each of M rounds I compute residuals, y minus the current prediction, which are the negative gradient of half squared error; fit a shallow regression tree to the residuals; and add learning rate times the tree's prediction to the running prediction, storing the tree. To predict on new data, I sum the initial mean plus learning rate times every tree's output. With two hundred depth two trees and a learning rate of 0.1 on a noisy sine wave, my loop's training MSE was 0.0203, identical to scikit-learn's implementation. For another loss I'd only change how the residuals and leaf values are computed.
must_mention: fit a shallow tree to residuals
store trees to predict new data

followups.q: How would you add early stopping?
followups.a: Track validation loss after each round and keep the number of trees where it was lowest.

followups.q: How would you change it for classification?
followups.a: Work in log odds, use residuals y minus sigmoid of F, and set leaf values by a Newton step.

q: How do the learning rate, the number of trees, early stopping and subsampling interact in gradient boosting?
plain: The learning rate, also called shrinkage, scales how much each new tree contributes. A small learning rate such as 0.05 needs more trees to fit the data but usually generalises better than a large one. That is because each tree only nudges the model. Boosting keeps reducing training error, so too many trees will overfit. So the number of trees is chosen by early stopping: stop when the validation error has not improved for a while. Training each tree on a random fraction of the rows, say 80 percent, adds randomness. That randomness also reduces overfitting and speeds training.
deep:
- **Shrinkage** $\nu \in (0, 1]$: $F_m = F_{m-1} + \nu h_m$. Smaller $\nu$ with more trees approximates a smoother path and generalises better (Friedman's empirical finding); cost is linear in the number of trees.
- **Number of trees $M$:** the main overfitting control; choose by early stopping on a validation set or CV (`n_iter_no_change`, `early_stopping_rounds`).
- **Row subsampling** (stochastic gradient boosting, `subsample` 0.5 to 0.8): variance reduction and speed; enables out of bag style estimates.
- **Column subsampling** (`colsample_bytree`, `max_features`): borrowed from random forests.
- **Tree complexity:** depth 3 to 8 or `num_leaves`; controls interaction order.
- **Leaf regularisation:** $\lambda$, $\gamma$, `min_child_weight` in XGBoost.
say: The learning rate scales each tree's contribution; it trades training time for generalisation, since smaller steps need more trees but usually give a better model. The number of trees is the main overfitting control in boosting, unlike in random forests, because training error keeps falling as trees are added. So I set a modest learning rate, like 0.05 or 0.1, and choose the number of trees with early stopping on a validation set. Subsampling rows for each tree, stochastic gradient boosting, adds randomness that reduces variance and speeds things up, and column subsampling does the same across features. Tree depth controls how many features can interact in a single tree.
must_mention: smaller learning rate needs more trees

followups.q: How do you select the number of trees in gradient boosting?
followups.a: Early stopping: monitor validation loss and keep the round with the best score.

followups.q: Is it possible to parallelise gradient boosting?
followups.a: Not across trees, which are sequential, but split finding within a tree parallelises over features and data blocks, which is what XGBoost and LightGBM do.

source.title: Alexey Grigorev, data science interview theory questions

q: Derive XGBoost's optimal leaf weight and split gain. Work an example.
plain: XGBoost (extreme gradient boosting) approximates the loss around the current predictions using both the slope (gradient) and the curvature (second derivative) for each example. XGBoost also adds a penalty for the number of leaves and for large leaf values. With a tree's structure fixed, each leaf's best value has a simple formula. The formula is minus the sum of gradients in the leaf, divided by the sum of curvatures plus the penalty lambda. For squared error the curvature is 1 per example. So a leaf holding residuals 3, 5 and 4 with lambda of 1 gets a value of 12 divided by 4, which is 3. The plain average would be 4. The same formula scores how good a split is.
deep:
Objective at round $t$ (Chen and Guestrin 2016, eq. 2 to 7): $\sum_i l(y_i, \hat y_i^{(t-1)} + f_t(x_i)) + \gamma T + \tfrac12\lambda\lVert w\rVert^2$. Second order Taylor with $g_i = \partial_{\hat y}l$, $h_i = \partial^2_{\hat y}l$:
$$\tilde L = \sum_{j=1}^T\Big[G_jw_j + \tfrac12(H_j + \lambda)w_j^2\Big] + \gamma T,\quad G_j = \sum_{i\in I_j}g_i,\ H_j = \sum_{i\in I_j}h_i.$$
Minimising per leaf: $w_j^\star = -\frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda}$, value $\tilde L^\star = -\tfrac12\sum_j\frac{G_j^2}{H_j + \lambda} + \gamma T$. Split gain:
$$\mathrm{Gain} = \tfrac12\Big[\frac{G_L^2}{H_L + \lambda} + \frac{G_R^2}{H_R + \lambda} - \frac{(G_L + G_R)^2}{H_L + H_R + \lambda}\Big] - \gamma.$$
Example (squared loss, $g_i = \hat y_i - y_i$, $h_i = 1$): targets 3, 5, 4 from $\hat y = 0$, $G = -12$, $H = 3$, $\lambda = 1$: $w^\star = 12/4 = 3$ (verified), shrunk from the mean 4. For log loss $g_i = p_i - y_i$, $h_i = p_i(1 - p_i)$. $\gamma$ acts as a minimum gain to split; `min_child_weight` bounds $H_j$.
say: XGBoost expands the loss to second order around the current predictions, using each row's gradient g and Hessian h, and adds gamma times the number of leaves plus one half lambda times the squared leaf weights. For a fixed tree structure the objective separates by leaf into G times w plus one half H plus lambda times w squared, so the optimal weight is minus G over H plus lambda, and plugging it back gives a score of minus one half G squared over H plus lambda per leaf. The split gain is half the sum of the children's scores minus the parent's, minus gamma. For squared loss, residuals of 3, 5 and 4 with lambda one give a weight of 3 instead of 4.
must_mention: second order Taylor expansion with g and h
penalty gamma T plus lambda over two times w squared
leaf weight minus G over H plus lambda
lambda shrinks leaves, gamma is a minimum gain

followups.q: What are g and h for log loss?
followups.a: g equals p minus y and h equals p times one minus p.

followups.q: What does min_child_weight constrain?
followups.a: The sum of Hessians in a child, roughly a minimum effective sample size per leaf.

source.title: Chen and Guestrin (2016), XGBoost

q: Beyond its objective, what engineering ideas made XGBoost fast and practical?
plain: XGBoost's speed came largely from systems ideas. XGBoost handles missing values by learning, at every split, which branch missing values should go down. The direction chosen is whichever lowers the loss more. Instead of trying every possible threshold, XGBoost can propose a smaller set of candidate thresholds. The candidates come from weighted quantiles (cut points that split the data into equal shares) of each feature. XGBoost also stores data in sorted, compressed column blocks that can be scanned in parallel and processed out of memory. Borrowing from random forests, XGBoost can sample columns for each tree to reduce overfitting.
deep:
From Chen and Guestrin (2016):
- **Sparsity aware split finding:** each node learns a default direction for missing (or zero) entries by evaluating both directions using only non missing statistics; the paper reports this running more than 50 times faster than a naive implementation on sparse data.
- **Approximate split finding:** candidate splits from percentiles; the **weighted quantile sketch** weights each point by its Hessian $h_i$, since the objective is a weighted squared loss with weights $h_i$. Global (once per tree) or local (per split) proposals.
- **Column block structure:** presorted compressed columns enable parallel split search; cache aware prefetching; block compression and sharding for out of core training.
- **Regularisation knobs:** shrinkage $\eta$, column subsampling, $\lambda$, $\alpha$ (L1 on leaves), $\gamma$, `min_child_weight`, `max_depth`. Default growth is level wise (depthwise).
say: Besides the regularised second order objective, the XGBoost paper's main contributions were systems ones. Sparsity aware split finding learns a default direction for missing values at each node by trying both and keeping the better, which the paper reports as more than fifty times faster than a naive approach on sparse data, and it means missing values need no imputation. An approximate algorithm proposes candidate thresholds from a weighted quantile sketch, weighting points by their Hessians. Data live in presorted, compressed column blocks, so split search parallelises across features and can run out of core. It also adds column subsampling and L1 and L2 penalties on leaf weights. Trees grow level by level by default.
must_mention: learned default direction for missing values
weighted quantile sketch for candidate splits
column blocks for parallel split search

followups.q: Do you need to impute missing values for XGBoost?
followups.a: No; it learns where missing values go at each split, though imputation can still help if missingness is not informative.

followups.q: Why weight quantiles by the Hessian?
followups.a: The second order objective is a squared loss weighted by h, so candidate splits should spread that weight evenly.

source.title: Chen and Guestrin (2016), XGBoost

q: What makes LightGBM fast? Explain histogram splits, leaf wise growth, GOSS and EFB.
plain: LightGBM (light gradient boosting machine) buckets each feature's values into a small number of bins. So finding a split means scanning about 255 bins rather than every distinct value. LightGBM grows trees leaf wise. Instead of splitting every node at the current depth, LightGBM always splits the single leaf that reduces the loss most. Leaf wise growth reaches lower error with fewer splits but can overfit small data, so the number of leaves must be capped. GOSS (gradient based one side sampling) keeps all examples with large gradients and only a random sample of the well fitted ones. EFB (exclusive feature bundling) bundles sparse features that are rarely nonzero together into one feature.
deep:
- **Histogram algorithm:** bin each feature (default up to 255 bins); split search costs $O(\#\text{bins})$ per feature; histogram subtraction (parent minus sibling) halves the work.
- **Leaf wise (best first) growth:** split the leaf with the largest gain; controlled by `num_leaves` (and `max_depth`, `min_data_in_leaf`); asymmetric deep trees, overfitting risk on small data.
- **GOSS** (gradient based one side sampling): keep the top $a$ fraction by $|g|$, sample $b$ of the rest and upweight them by $(1 - a)/b$ to keep gain estimates unbiased.
