- **EFB** (exclusive feature bundling): bundle mutually exclusive sparse features; optimal bundling is NP hard, a greedy algorithm works well.
- Native categorical handling via gradient statistics per category.

Ke et al. (NeurIPS 2017) report training up to over 20 times faster than conventional GBDT with almost the same accuracy. sklearn's `HistGradientBoosting` uses the same histogram idea.
say: LightGBM's speed comes from four ideas. Histograms: each feature is binned into at most a couple of hundred buckets, so split search scans bins instead of sorted values, and a child's histogram can be computed by subtracting its sibling's from the parent's. Leaf wise growth: it always splits the leaf with the biggest gain rather than growing level by level, which is efficient but can overfit small datasets, so num_leaves is the key parameter to constrain. GOSS keeps rows with large gradients and samples the small gradient ones, reweighting them. EFB bundles sparse features that are rarely nonzero together. The paper reports up to over twenty times faster training at similar accuracy.

followups.q: Why can leaf wise growth overfit?
followups.a: It can build very deep, narrow branches chasing a few examples; cap num_leaves, max_depth and min_data_in_leaf.

followups.q: What sklearn model uses the same histogram idea?
followups.a: HistGradientBoostingClassifier and HistGradientBoostingRegressor.

source.title: Ke et al. (2017), LightGBM

q: What target leakage does CatBoost fix? Explain ordered target statistics and prediction shift.
plain: A common way to use a categorical feature is to replace each category with the average target of rows in that category. But a row's own label is included in its own average, which leaks the answer. If every category were unique, the encoded value would just be a smoothed copy of the label. Then training accuracy would be perfect, and test accuracy would be a coin flip. CatBoost fixes this target leakage by shuffling the rows and encoding each row using only the rows before it in that random order. So no row ever sees its own label. CatBoost applies the same idea to boosting itself, computing each row's residual with a model that did not train on that row.
deep:
Greedy target statistic $\hat x_k = \frac{\sum_j\mathbb{1}\{x_j = x_k\}y_j + ap}{\sum_j\mathbb{1}\{x_j = x_k\} + a}$ includes $y_k$, causing conditional shift: the distribution of $\hat x\mid y$ differs between train and test. Prokhorenkova et al.'s example: unique categories with $P(y = 1) = 0.5$ give a perfectly separating threshold on training data and 0.5 accuracy on test. Leave one out encoding still leaks (a constant feature becomes a function of $y_k$).

Ordered TS: random permutation $\sigma$, use only $D_k = \{x_j : \sigma(j) < \sigma(k)\}$ for training rows (the full data for test rows); multiple permutations reduce variance for early rows.

Prediction shift: gradients for row $k$ come from a model trained on row $k$, so $F_{t-1}(x_k)\mid x_k$ is shifted relative to test points; ordered boosting maintains supporting models on permutation prefixes so residuals are unbiased. CatBoost also uses oblivious (symmetric) trees: one split per depth level, fast and less prone to overfitting.
say: Target encoding replaces a category with the mean target of its rows, but that mean includes the row's own label, which is leakage. The CatBoost paper's extreme example: if every category is unique, the encoding is a smoothed copy of y, one split classifies the training set perfectly, and test accuracy is fifty percent. Even leave one out encoding leaks. CatBoost's fix is ordered target statistics: randomly permute the rows and encode each one using only the rows that come before it, like an online learner, using several permutations to reduce variance. Prediction shift is the same problem inside boosting: residuals are computed with a model that saw the row, so CatBoost's ordered boosting computes them with models trained on earlier rows only.
must_mention: target encoding includes the row's own label
ordered target statistics over a permutation

followups.q: How would you target encode safely without CatBoost?
followups.a: Compute encodings out of fold, with smoothing toward the global mean, inside the cross validation loop.

followups.q: What are oblivious trees?
followups.a: Trees that use the same split at every node of a level, giving balanced, fast, regularised trees.

source.title: Prokhorenkova et al., CatBoost

q: Compare XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost. How would you choose?
plain: XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost are all gradient boosted tree libraries with similar accuracy when tuned. So the differences are mostly speed, defaults and categorical handling. XGBoost is the mature, widely deployed baseline with a regularised objective and good missing value handling. LightGBM is usually the fastest on large datasets thanks to histograms and leaf wise growth. LightGBM needs its number of leaves constrained on small data. CatBoost shines when there are many categorical features, such as city, device and merchant identifiers, because its ordered encoding avoids leakage. CatBoost's defaults also often work well without tuning.
deep:
| | XGBoost | LightGBM | CatBoost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Split finding | exact or histogram, weighted quantile sketch | histogram, GOSS, EFB | histogram on oblivious trees |
| Growth | level wise (depthwise) default | leaf wise, `num_leaves` | symmetric, one split per level |
| Categoricals | encode yourself (newer versions add native support) | native, gradient statistics | ordered target statistics |
| Missing values | learned default direction | learned default direction | handled natively |
| Signature idea | second order regularised objective | speed | removing target leakage and prediction shift |
| Watch out | many knobs | overfits small data | slower training, larger models |

Choosing: try LightGBM for speed on big data, CatBoost for many high cardinality categoricals or little tuning time, XGBoost as the standard well supported option; benchmark on your validation set, since results vary by dataset.
say: They're all gradient boosted trees, and with tuning their accuracy is usually close, so I choose on data shape and practicalities. XGBoost is the established workhorse: second order regularised objective, learned handling of missing values, level wise trees by default, lots of deployment support. LightGBM is typically fastest on large data because of histograms, gradient based sampling and feature bundling, and it grows trees leaf wise, so I constrain num_leaves on small data. CatBoost is my pick with many high cardinality categoricals, since ordered target statistics avoid target leakage, and its defaults are strong out of the box, at the cost of slower training. Whatever I pick, I'd confirm on my own validation set.
must_mention: LightGBM speed and leaf wise growth

followups.q: How do you approach tuning XGBoost or LightGBM?
followups.a: Fix a learning rate, early stop the number of trees, then tune tree complexity, then sampling, then leaf penalties.

followups.q: What are the main parameters in gradient boosting?
followups.a: Learning rate, number of trees, depth or leaves, minimum child weight, subsampling and leaf regularisation.

source.title: Alexey Grigorev, data science interview theory questions

q: What is the difference between a random forest and gradient boosting, and when would you use each?
plain: A random forest grows many deep trees independently on bootstrap samples and averages them. Gradient boosting grows many shallow trees one after another, each correcting the ensemble's remaining errors. Forests are hard to break: few settings matter, more trees never hurt, and training runs in parallel. Boosting usually reaches higher accuracy on tabular data. But boosting needs tuning of the learning rate, tree depth and number of trees, and overfits if you keep adding trees. A good habit is a random forest as a quick, solid baseline. Use gradient boosting when you need the last few points of accuracy.
deep:
| | Random forest | Gradient boosting |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trees | deep, independent | shallow (depth 3 to 8), sequential |
| Error reduced | variance | bias (and variance via shrinkage) |
| More trees | converges | overfits without early stopping |
| Tuning sensitivity | low | high |
| Parallelism | across trees | within a tree (split search) only |
| Validation | OOB for free | needs a validation set or CV |
| Noise and outliers | tolerant | less tolerant with some losses |
| Probabilities | pulled from 0 and 1 | usually better calibrated with log loss, still check |

Both: no scaling, handle interactions, cannot extrapolate.
say: A random forest averages deep, independently grown trees, each on a bootstrap sample with random features per split, so it attacks variance; gradient boosting adds shallow trees sequentially, each fit to the current errors, so it attacks bias. Practically, forests are hard to break and low maintenance: few hyperparameters matter, more trees never hurt, they parallelise across trees and give out of bag error for free. Boosting is usually more accurate on tabular data but sensitive to learning rate, depth and number of trees, needs early stopping, and only parallelises within a tree. My workflow is a forest as a quick strong baseline, then tuned boosting if the extra accuracy is worth it.
must_mention: deep independent versus shallow sequential trees
forest hard to break and parallel
boosting more accurate but tuning sensitive

followups.q: What's the difference between random forest and gradient boosting?
followups.a: Independent deep trees averaged versus sequential shallow trees fit to residuals.

followups.q: Is it possible to parallelise gradient boosting?
followups.a: Within each tree, yes, by parallel split finding over features or data shards; trees themselves are sequential.

source.title: Alexey Grigorev, data science interview theory questions

q: What problems is gradient boosting good for, and when would you not use it?
plain: Gradient boosted trees are the default winner for tabular data: rows of customers, transactions or sensors. Such data has a mix of numeric and categorical columns, missing values and nonlinear interactions, as in fraud detection, credit risk, churn and ranking. Gradient boosted trees need no feature scaling and handle missing values natively. Gradient boosted trees are a poor fit for raw images, audio or text, where neural networks learn the features. They are also a poor fit for tiny datasets, where a regularised linear model is safer. They are also a poor fit for problems needing extrapolation beyond the training range. They are also a poor fit where you need a model whose coefficients you can explain directly.
deep:
Good for: heterogeneous tabular features, nonlinear interactions, moderate to large $n$, missing values, ranking (LambdaMART style objectives), quantile and custom losses, strong baselines in competitions and industry.

Less suitable:
- Unstructured data (images, audio, raw text): use neural networks or embeddings as features.
- Extrapolation in time or feature space: trees predict within the training range; detrend or use linear components.
- Very small $n$ or $d \gg n$ sparse text: regularised linear models or naive Bayes often match or win.
- Strict latency or memory: many trees cost time; distil or prune.
- Need for smooth, monotone or interpretable relationships: use monotone constraints, GAMs, or linear models.
- Streaming updates: retraining is batch oriented.
say: Boosted trees are what I reach for first on tabular data with mixed feature types, missing values and nonlinear interactions: fraud, credit risk, churn, pricing, click prediction and learning to rank. They need no scaling, take custom losses, and handle missingness natively. I wouldn't use them on raw unstructured data like images, audio or text, where neural networks learn the representation, though boosting on top of embeddings can work. They can't extrapolate beyond the training range, which matters for trends. With very little data or very wide sparse text, a regularised linear model is often as good and much simpler. And for a strictly interpretable model I'd consider monotone constraints or a GAM.
must_mention: small or sparse data favours linear models

followups.q: Would you prefer gradient boosting or logistic regression for bag of words text classification?
followups.a: Usually logistic regression: very wide sparse features suit linear models, and boosting gains little for the cost.

followups.q: What algorithms would you use to prototype a fraud model?
followups.a: Logistic regression as a baseline, then gradient boosted trees with class weights and a PR based metric.

source.title: Chip Huyen, ML Interviews Book, classic ML questions

q: How does k-means work, and does it always converge?
plain: The k-means algorithm splits data into k groups. The algorithm starts with k centre points and assigns every data point to its nearest centre. The algorithm then moves each centre to the average of the points assigned to it. The algorithm repeats these two steps until the assignments stop changing. Each of those two steps can only lower the total squared distance from points to their centres, so the algorithm always settles. But it can settle in a poor arrangement depending on where the centres started. So you run it several times from different starts and keep the best. The algorithm assumes roughly round, similarly sized clusters.
deep:
Objective (distortion, inertia): $J(c, \mu) = \sum_i\lVert x_i - \mu_{c_i}\rVert^2$.
Lloyd's algorithm alternates: $c_i := \arg\min_j\lVert x_i - \mu_j\rVert^2$ (minimise over $c$), $\mu_j := \text{mean of points with } c_i = j$ (minimise over $\mu$). This is coordinate descent on $J$, so $J$ is monotone non increasing and converges (CS229 chapter 10); verified numerically over 10 iterations. $J$ is non convex, so only a local optimum is reached; exact minimisation is NP hard even for $k = 2$.

Cost $O(nkd)$ per iteration. Assumptions: convex, isotropic clusters of similar size and density; scale features; Euclidean distance. Mini batch k-means trades a little quality for speed. k-means is the limit of a GMM with shared spherical covariance shrinking to zero.
say: k-means alternates two steps. Assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its assigned points, and repeat until assignments stop changing. Both steps exactly minimise the total within cluster squared distance, one over assignments and one over centroids, so it's coordinate descent and the objective can never increase, which guarantees convergence. But the objective isn't convex, so it converges to a local optimum that depends on initialisation; I run it several times, or use k-means plus plus seeding, and keep the lowest inertia. Each iteration costs n times k times d. It implicitly assumes round, similar sized clusters, so I scale features first.
must_mention: assign to nearest centroid, recompute means

followups.q: Is k-means guaranteed to find the global optimum?
followups.a: No; the problem is NP hard and Lloyd's algorithm finds a local optimum.

followups.q: What does k-means assume about clusters?
followups.a: Roughly spherical, similar size and density, in a space where Euclidean distance is meaningful.

source.title: Alexey Grigorev, data science interview theory questions

q: What is k-means++, and what does it guarantee?
plain: The k-means++ method is a smarter way to pick the starting centres. The first centre is a random data point. Each later centre is chosen at random with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest centre already chosen. So far away points are likely picks, and the starting centres spread across the data. On average, k-means++ alone gives a clustering that is provably within a factor proportional to the log of k of the best possible. In a test with 15 clusters, single runs from k-means++ starts averaged about a third lower error than random starts.
deep:
Seeding (Arthur and Vassilvitskii, SODA 2007):
1. Pick $\mu_1$ uniformly from the data.
2. For each $x$, $D(x)$ = distance to the nearest chosen centre; pick the next centre with probability $D(x)^2/\sum_{x'}D(x')^2$.
3. Repeat until $k$ centres; then run Lloyd's algorithm.

Guarantee: the expected cost after seeding is $O(\log k)$ times optimal; the paper shows the bound is tight, $\Theta(\log k)$ competitive. Verified: on 15 well separated blobs, mean single initialisation inertia 1259.9 (k-means++) against 1853.4 (random). sklearn uses `init="k-means++"` by default; still use several restarts (`n_init`). Cost $O(nkd)$ for seeding, inherently sequential (k-means|| parallelises it).
say: k-means plus plus is an initialisation scheme. I pick the first centroid uniformly at random, then pick each subsequent centroid from the data with probability proportional to its squared distance to the nearest centroid already chosen, the D squared weighting. That spreads the initial centroids out and makes it unlikely to put two seeds in one true cluster. Arthur and Vassilvitskii proved the expected cost of the seeding alone is within a log k factor of the optimum, before Lloyd's iterations even run. In a quick fifteen cluster test, k-means plus plus seeds gave about a third lower inertia per run than random seeds. It's sklearn's default, though I still use several restarts.
must_mention: next centre with probability proportional to squared distance

followups.q: Why squared distance rather than distance?
followups.a: It matches the k-means objective and is what the proof uses; it favours far points strongly.

followups.q: Is k-means++ seeding parallelisable?
followups.a: Not directly; k-means parallel (k-means||) oversamples in a few rounds to parallelise it.

source.title: Arthur and Vassilvitskii (2007), k-means++

q: How do you choose k for k-means?
plain: There is no single correct method for choosing k, so use several and expect them to disagree sometimes. The total within cluster distance always falls as k rises, so look for an elbow where adding clusters stops helping much. The silhouette score compares how close each point is to its own cluster versus the next nearest one, and peaks at a good k. For data generated from 4 groups, the silhouette peaked at k equal to 4. A Gaussian mixture's BIC (Bayesian information criterion, a score that penalises complex models) preferred 3 because two groups overlapped. Business usefulness and stability across resamples matter as much as any score.
deep:
- **Elbow:** inertia versus $k$ (verified: 2922 at $k = 2$ down to 810 at $k = 6$, monotone). Subjective.
- **Silhouette:** $s_i = \frac{b_i - a_i}{\max(a_i, b_i)}$, $a_i$ mean intra cluster distance, $b_i$ mean distance to the nearest other cluster; average in $[-1, 1]$. Verified peak 0.500 at $k = 4$.
- **BIC or AIC** for GMMs (verified: BIC 4942.2 at $k = 3$ versus 4953.0 at $k = 4$).
- **Gap statistic:** compare $\log W_k$ with its expectation under a uniform reference.
- **Stability:** cluster bootstrap resamples, compare labelings with adjusted Rand index.
- Calinski Harabasz (higher better), Davies Bouldin (lower better). All favour convex clusters.

Choose with domain constraints (how many segments can marketing act on).
say: I combine several signals because none is decisive. The elbow in inertia against k is the classic one, but inertia always decreases, so the elbow is a judgement call. The silhouette score, b minus a over the max of the two, where a is the mean distance to my own cluster and b to the nearest other cluster, should peak at a good k. For a Gaussian mixture I'd use BIC. On data generated with four blobs, the silhouette peaked at four but BIC preferred three, because two blobs overlapped, which is a good reminder that criteria disagree. Then I check stability across resamples and whether the segments are actionable.
must_mention: silhouette b minus a over max

followups.q: How would you choose the value of k?
followups.a: Elbow, silhouette, BIC or gap statistic, stability, and domain constraints together.

followups.q: What do silhouette scores near zero mean?
followups.a: Points sit on the boundary between clusters; negative means likely misassigned.

source.title: Chip Huyen, ML Interviews Book, classic ML questions

q: How do you evaluate a clustering when labels are known, and when they are not?
plain: If true labels exist, compare the clusters with the labels using a score that ignores the arbitrary cluster numbering and corrects for chance agreement. An example is the adjusted Rand index, where 1 is perfect and about 0 is random. On two interlocking crescent shapes, k-means scored 0.25 and DBSCAN (a density based clustering method) scored 1.0. Without labels, use internal scores such as the silhouette. Also check whether the clusters stay the same when you resample the data. Above all, test whether the clusters are useful, for example whether customer segments respond differently to the same campaign.
deep:
External (labels available), permutation invariant:
- Adjusted Rand index: $\frac{RI - \mathbb{E}[RI]}{\max RI - \mathbb{E}[RI]}$, about 0 for random, 1 for identical; unadjusted RI stays near 1 even for different labelings.
- Adjusted mutual information; homogeneity, completeness and V measure; Fowlkes Mallows.

Internal (no labels): silhouette, Calinski Harabasz, Davies Bouldin, inertia, BIC. Caveat: they favour convex, compact clusters and mislead for density based or non convex shapes.

Other evidence: stability under bootstrap or subsampling (ARI between runs), agreement across algorithms, and downstream or business validation (lift in a targeted action, interpretability of segment profiles).
say: With labels I use an external index that's invariant to how clusters are numbered and corrected for chance, like the adjusted Rand index or adjusted mutual information; ARI is near zero for random labelings and one for perfect agreement. For example, on the two moons dataset k-means scored about 0.25 and DBSCAN 1.0. Without labels I use internal criteria like silhouette or Calinski Harabasz, remembering they favour compact convex clusters, so they can penalise a perfectly good density based clustering. Then I check stability, rerunning on bootstrap samples and comparing labelings, and finally usefulness: do the segments differ meaningfully and respond differently to an action?
must_mention: adjusted Rand index or adjusted mutual information
invariant to label permutation and chance corrected

followups.q: If the labels are known, how would you evaluate k-means?
followups.a: Adjusted Rand index or adjusted mutual information against the labels.

followups.q: Why not plain accuracy?
followups.a: Cluster IDs are arbitrary; you would need an optimal matching, and accuracy ignores chance agreement.

source.title: Chip Huyen, ML Interviews Book, classic ML questions

q: What is a Gaussian mixture model, how does EM fit it, and how does it compare with k-means?
plain: A Gaussian mixture model assumes the data come from several bell shaped clusters, each with its own centre, shape and share of the data. You do not know which cluster produced each point. The EM (expectation maximisation) algorithm alternates two steps. First, EM estimates for each point the probability that each cluster produced it. Second, EM refits each cluster's centre, shape and share, using those probabilities as soft weights. Compared with k-means, a Gaussian mixture allows oval and differently sized clusters. A Gaussian mixture also gives each point a probability of membership rather than a hard label, at higher cost. The k-means algorithm is the special case with round, equal clusters and hard assignments.
deep:
Model: $z_i \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}(\phi)$, $x_i\mid z_i = j \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_j, \Sigma_j)$, $z$ latent.
- **E step:** $w_{ij} = p(z_i = j\mid x_i) = \frac{\phi_j\mathcal{N}(x_i;\mu_j, \Sigma_j)}{\sum_l\phi_l\mathcal{N}(x_i;\mu_l, \Sigma_l)}$.
- **M step:** $\phi_j = \frac1n\sum_iw_{ij}$, $\mu_j = \frac{\sum_iw_{ij}x_i}{\sum_iw_{ij}}$, $\Sigma_j = \frac{\sum_iw_{ij}(x_i - \mu_j)(x_i - \mu_j)^\top}{\sum_iw_{ij}}$ (GDA's estimates with soft labels).

Versus k-means: soft versus hard assignment; elliptical, unequal clusters via $\Sigma_j$; a density model (likelihood, BIC, sampling, anomaly scores); more parameters ($O(kd^2)$ with full covariances), slower, can collapse onto a single point (infinite likelihood), hence `reg_covar`. Both find local optima; initialise GMMs with k-means. k-means is the limit $\Sigma_j = \sigma^2I$, $\sigma \to 0$.
say: A GMM models the data as a weighted mixture of Gaussians, each with its own mean and covariance, where the component that generated each point is hidden. EM fits it by alternating an E step, computing each point's responsibility under each component with Bayes' rule, and an M step, re-estimating the weights, means and covariances as responsibility weighted averages, which are just GDA's formulas with soft labels. Compared with k-means, a GMM gives soft memberships, handles elliptical and unequal clusters, and is a proper density model, so I get likelihoods and BIC. It's slower, has more parameters, and can collapse onto single points without covariance regularisation. k-means is the hard, spherical limit.
must_mention: mixture of Gaussians with latent component
E step responsibilities by Bayes rule
M step weighted means and covariances
soft and elliptical versus hard and spherical

followups.q: Compare k-means and GMM.
followups.a: Hard versus soft assignments, spherical versus elliptical clusters, distortion versus likelihood; GMM is costlier and gives densities.

followups.q: When would you choose a GMM over k-means?
followups.a: When clusters are elongated or of different sizes, or you need membership probabilities or a density.

source.title: Chip Huyen, ML Interviews Book, classic ML questions

q: Why does each EM iteration never decrease the likelihood? Derive the evidence lower bound.
plain: EM (expectation maximisation) never makes the likelihood worse, because each iteration builds a lower bound on the log likelihood that touches it exactly at the current parameters. EM then moves the parameters to the top of that bound. The new likelihood must be at least the bound's new value, which is at least the bound's old value, which equals the old likelihood. The bound comes from Jensen's inequality: the log of an average is at least the average of the logs. The bound is called the evidence lower bound. The bound is tight when the weighting distribution equals the posterior over the hidden variables. That posterior is exactly what the E step computes.
deep:
For any distribution $Q$ over latent $z$ (CS229 section 11.3):
$$\log p(x;\theta) = \log\sum_zQ(z)\frac{p(x, z;\theta)}{Q(z)} \ge \sum_zQ(z)\log\frac{p(x, z;\theta)}{Q(z)} = \mathrm{ELBO}(Q, \theta),$$
by Jensen on the concave log. Equality iff $p(x, z;\theta)/Q(z)$ is constant in $z$, i.e. $Q(z) = p(z\mid x;\theta)$. Equivalently $\mathrm{ELBO} = \log p(x;\theta) - \mathrm{KL}(Q\,\Vert\,p(z\mid x;\theta))$.

EM: E step $Q^{(t)} = p(z\mid x;\theta^{(t)})$; M step $\theta^{(t+1)} = \arg\max_\theta\mathrm{ELBO}(Q^{(t)}, \theta)$. Then
$$\ell(\theta^{(t+1)}) \ge \mathrm{ELBO}(Q^{(t)}, \theta^{(t+1)}) \ge \mathrm{ELBO}(Q^{(t)}, \theta^{(t)}) = \ell(\theta^{(t)}).$$
Coordinate ascent on the ELBO; converges to a stationary point (local optimum), not necessarily global. Verified: GMM log likelihood was monotone over 30 iterations. Variational inference and VAEs maximise the same ELBO with a restricted $Q$.
say: For any distribution Q over the latent variables, I can write log p of x as the log of an expectation under Q of p of x and z over Q of z. Since log is concave, Jensen's inequality says that's at least the expectation of the log, which is the evidence lower bound. The gap is the KL divergence between Q and the true posterior over z, so the bound is tight exactly when Q equals the posterior. The E step sets Q to the posterior, making the bound touch the likelihood at the current parameters; the M step maximises the bound over the parameters. So the new likelihood is at least the new bound, which is at least the old bound, which equals the old likelihood.
must_mention: gap is KL to the posterior
E step makes the bound tight
M step maximises the bound, so likelihood never decreases

followups.q: Does EM find the global maximum?
followups.a: No, only a stationary point; restarts and k-means initialisation help.

followups.q: How does this relate to variational autoencoders?
followups.a: VAEs maximise the same ELBO with an amortised, parametric Q from an encoder network.

source.title: Stanford CS229 main notes, Spring 2026

q: How does DBSCAN work?
plain: DBSCAN (density based spatial clustering of applications with noise) finds clusters as dense regions separated by sparse ones. A point is a core point if at least a minimum number of points, say 5, lie within a radius eps of it. Clusters grow by linking core points that are within eps of each other. Points near a core point but not dense themselves join as border points. Anything else is labelled noise. DBSCAN needs no number of clusters, finds clusters of any shape, and flags outliers. But one radius cannot fit clusters of very different densities.
deep:
Parameters: `eps` (neighbourhood radius), `min_samples` (density threshold).
- Core point: $|N_\epsilon(x)| \ge$ `min_samples`.
- Border point: within $\epsilon$ of a core point but not core.
- Noise: neither; label $-1$.
Clusters are maximal sets of density connected points.

Properties (sklearn guide): arbitrary shapes, no $k$, outlier detection; deterministic for fixed data order except that border points reachable from two clusters go to whichever is found first; tree indexes make it scale well, but sparse input can force $O(n^2)$ memory. Choosing `eps`: knee of the sorted $k$ distance plot with $k$ = `min_samples`. Fails with varying density; HDBSCAN builds the hierarchy over all density levels and removes `eps`. Verified: two moons ARI 1.0 for DBSCAN versus 0.253 for k-means.
say: DBSCAN is density based. A point is a core point if at least min_samples points lie within distance eps of it. Clusters are formed by chaining together core points that are within eps of each other, border points within eps of a core point get attached, and everything else is labelled noise. So I don't choose the number of clusters, clusters can take any shape, and outliers are flagged automatically: on the two moons dataset it recovered both shapes perfectly where k-means scored an ARI of about 0.25. I'd set eps from the knee of a sorted k nearest neighbour distance plot. Its weakness is varying density, where HDBSCAN works better.
must_mention: core points with min_samples within eps
struggles with varying density, use HDBSCAN

followups.q: Do you know how DBSCAN works?
followups.a: Core points within eps of at least min_samples neighbours, density connected into clusters, the rest noise.

followups.q: How do you choose eps?
followups.a: Plot each point's distance to its k th nearest neighbour sorted, and pick the knee.

source.title: scikit-learn: clustering

q: When would you choose k-means and when DBSCAN?
plain: Choose k-means when you expect roughly round, similarly sized groups, know about how many you want, and need speed on large data. An example is splitting customers into five segments for a campaign. Choose DBSCAN (a density based clustering method) when clusters may have odd shapes and you do not know how many there are. Also choose DBSCAN when you want outliers left out rather than forced into a group. An example is finding hotspots of GPS (global positioning system) points along roads. The k-means algorithm assigns every point to some cluster, which drags centres toward outliers. DBSCAN struggles when cluster densities differ a lot and when the data have many dimensions.
deep:
| | k-means | DBSCAN |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Needs $k$ | yes | no (needs `eps`, `min_samples`) |
| Cluster shape | convex, isotropic | arbitrary |
| Outliers | assigned, distort centroids | labelled noise |
| Density variation | tolerates (if spherical) | struggles (use HDBSCAN) |
| New points | assign to nearest centroid | no native predict (transductive) |
| Scale | very large $n$ (mini batch) | large $n$ with indexes |
| High dimensions | degrades | degrades more (distance based density) |
| Determinism | depends on initialisation | deterministic up to border points |
say: I'd pick k-means when I expect compact, roughly spherical clusters, have a sense of k, need to scale to lots of data, and want to assign new points easily to the nearest centroid, like defining a handful of customer segments. I'd pick DBSCAN when clusters could be irregularly shaped, I don't know how many there are, and I want noise identified rather than forced into a cluster, like spatial hotspots or anomaly screening. k-means is pulled around by outliers because every point must belong somewhere. DBSCAN breaks down when densities vary widely, where HDBSCAN is better, and both suffer in high dimensions, so I'd reduce dimension first.
must_mention: k-means for spherical clusters with known k
DBSCAN for arbitrary shapes and unknown k

followups.q: Can DBSCAN predict clusters for new points?
followups.a: Not natively; assign new points to the cluster of a nearby core point, or refit.

followups.q: What other clustering algorithms do you know?
followups.a: GMMs, hierarchical clustering, HDBSCAN, spectral clustering, mean shift, BIRCH.

source.title: Alexey Grigorev, data science interview theory questions

q: How does hierarchical agglomerative clustering work, and how do the linkage choices differ?
plain: Agglomerative clustering starts with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters until one remains. The merges are recorded as a tree called a dendrogram. Cutting the tree at a chosen height gives any number of clusters, so you do not need to fix k in advance. The linkage rule defines distance between clusters. Single linkage uses the closest pair of points and tends to chain clusters into long strings. Complete linkage uses the farthest pair, and average linkage uses the mean distance. Ward's method merges whichever pair increases within cluster variance least, which behaves like k-means.
deep:
Algorithm: start with $n$ singletons; merge the closest pair under linkage $D(A, B)$; update distances; repeat. Naive cost $O(n^3)$, $O(n^2)$ memory for the distance matrix (efficient variants $O(n^2)$ time).

Linkages (sklearn guide):
- Single: $\min_{a\in A, b\in B}d(a, b)$; finds non globular shapes, chaining, brittle with noise; equivalent to a minimum spanning tree.
- Complete: $\max d(a, b)$; compact clusters, sensitive to outliers.
- Average: mean pairwise distance; works with non Euclidean metrics.
- Ward: merge minimising the increase in total within cluster sum of squares; Euclidean only; most regular sizes.

Connectivity constraints (a k nearest neighbour graph) restrict merges to neighbours and speed it up, but can amplify rich get richer effects with single, average or complete linkage. Divisive (top down) clustering is the reverse.
say: Agglomerative clustering is bottom up: every point starts as its own cluster, and I repeatedly merge the two closest clusters, producing a dendrogram that I can cut at any height to get any number of clusters. The linkage defines cluster distance. Single linkage uses the closest pair, which can find elongated shapes but chains clusters together through noise. Complete linkage uses the farthest pair and gives compact clusters but is sensitive to outliers. Average linkage uses the mean pairwise distance and works with any metric. Ward merges the pair that least increases within cluster variance, behaves like k-means and gives balanced sizes. The catch is quadratic memory for the distance matrix.

followups.q: When is hierarchical clustering preferable to k-means?
followups.a: When you want the whole hierarchy, a non Euclidean metric, or no fixed k, on moderate n.

followups.q: Why can't Ward use cosine distance?
followups.a: Its variance based merge criterion is defined for Euclidean distance.

source.title: scikit-learn: clustering

q: What does PCA do? Derive the first principal component as a variance maximisation problem.
plain: PCA (principal component analysis) finds the directions in which the data spread out the most, and lets you keep just the top few. Picture a cloud of points shaped like a tilted cigar. The first principal component is the cigar's long axis. The second principal component is the widest direction at right angles to it, and so on. Projecting onto the first two or three directions keeps most of the spread while dropping the rest. Mathematically, the best direction turns out to be the top eigenvector of the data's covariance matrix (a table of how features vary together). An eigenvector is a direction that the matrix only stretches, and the variance it captures is the matching eigenvalue.
deep:
Centre the data (and standardise if units differ, CS229 chapter 12). For a unit vector $u$, the variance of projections $x_i^\top u$ is $\frac1n\sum_i(x_i^\top u)^2 = u^\top\Sigma u$ with $\Sigma = \frac1n\sum_ix_ix_i^\top$.

Maximise $u^\top\Sigma u$ s.t. $u^\top u = 1$. Lagrangian $u^\top\Sigma u - \lambda(u^\top u - 1)$; gradient $2\Sigma u - 2\lambda u = 0 \Rightarrow \Sigma u = \lambda u$. At a stationary point the variance is $u^\top\Sigma u = \lambda$, so pick the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue. The top $k$ eigenvectors (orthogonal, since $\Sigma$ is symmetric) span the best $k$ dimensional subspace, and the scores $y_i = (u_1^\top x_i, \dots, u_k^\top x_i)$ are the reduced representation. Equivalently, PCA minimises squared reconstruction error, and the error equals the sum of discarded eigenvalues.
say: PCA finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance and projects the data onto the top few. To derive the first one, I centre the data and look for a unit vector u maximising the variance of the projections, which is u transpose sigma u, where sigma is the covariance matrix. With a Lagrange multiplier for the unit norm constraint, setting the gradient to zero gives sigma u equals lambda u, so u must be an eigenvector, and the variance achieved equals its eigenvalue. So the first principal component is the top eigenvector, and the top k eigenvectors give the best k dimensional subspace. The same subspace minimises squared reconstruction error.
must_mention: maximise u transpose sigma u with unit norm

followups.q: Why are the components orthogonal?
followups.a: The covariance matrix is symmetric, so its eigenvectors can be chosen orthogonal.

followups.q: What are the uses of PCA?
followups.a: Compression, visualisation, denoising, decorrelating features, and reducing dimension before another model.

source.title: Stanford CS229 main notes, Spring 2026

q: How is PCA computed with the SVD, and what is explained variance?
plain: In practice, PCA (principal component analysis) is computed with the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the centred data matrix. The SVD gives the same directions as the covariance eigenvectors without forming the covariance, and it is more numerically stable. Each component's eigenvalue is its variance. A component's explained variance ratio is its eigenvalue divided by the total. In a five feature example, the first two components explained 49 and 27 percent of the variance, 75 percent together. The information lost by dropping the other three components equalled exactly the sum of their eigenvalues. You pick the number of components where a scree plot (a chart of eigenvalues) levels off. Or you pick the number where the cumulative share reaches, say, 90 to 95 percent.
deep:
Centred $X_c = USV^\top$: columns of $V$ are principal directions, eigenvalues $\lambda_j = s_j^2/(n - 1)$, scores $X_cV = US$. Avoids forming $X^\top X$, which squares the condition number. Cost $O(nd\min(n, d))$; randomised SVD for the top $k$.

Explained variance ratio $\lambda_j/\sum_l\lambda_l$; reconstruction error of a rank $k$ projection $= \sum_{j>k}\lambda_j$.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Z = rng.normal(size=(400, 5)) @ rng.normal(size=(5, 5))
Zc = Z - Z.mean(axis=0)
eig = np.linalg.eigvalsh(np.cov(Zc, rowvar=False))[::-1]
s = np.linalg.svd(Zc, compute_uv=False)
print(eig.round(3), (s**2 / (len(Z) - 1)).round(3))   # both [11.601 6.308 5.597 0.21 0.023]
pca = PCA(n_components=2).fit(Z)
print(pca.explained_variance_ratio_.round(3))           # [0.489 0.266]
rec = pca.inverse_transform(pca.transform(Z))
print(round(((Z - rec) ** 2).sum() / (len(Z) - 1), 4), round(eig[2:].sum(), 4))  # 5.8303 5.8303
```
say: I'd compute PCA from the SVD of the centred data matrix: X equals U S V transpose, the columns of V are the principal directions, the eigenvalues of the covariance are the squared singular values over n minus one, and the scores are U times S. It's more stable than forming X transpose X, which squares the condition number. Each component's explained variance ratio is its eigenvalue over the sum of all eigenvalues. In a quick example, two of five components explained about 49 and 27 percent, and the reconstruction error from dropping the rest equalled exactly the sum of the three dropped eigenvalues. I choose k from a scree plot elbow or a cumulative threshold like ninety five percent.
must_mention: V gives directions, s squared over n minus one gives variances
choose k by scree or cumulative share

followups.q: What is singular value decomposition, and how is it used in ML?
followups.a: X equals U S V transpose; used for PCA, low rank approximation, latent semantic analysis, recommender matrix factorisation and pseudo inverses.

followups.q: Why must you centre before PCA?
followups.a: Otherwise the first component points toward the mean rather than along the direction of greatest spread.

source.title: Alexey Grigorev, data science interview theory questions

q: What are the pitfalls of PCA, and when should you not use it?
plain: PCA (principal component analysis) is sensitive to units. A feature measured in metres has a million times the variance of the same feature in kilometres. So without standardising, PCA just picks the large unit features. PCA only finds straight line structure, so a spiral or curved surface is not captured. PCA keeps directions with the most spread, which are not necessarily the most useful for predicting your target. A quiet direction can be the predictive one. In a modelling pipeline, PCA must be fitted on the training data only, or it leaks information from the test set.
deep:
- **Scale:** standardise unless features share units (pixel intensities can skip it).
- **Linearity:** captures linear correlations only; use kernel PCA, autoencoders, or manifold methods for nonlinear structure.
- **Unsupervised:** ignores $y$; principal components regression can discard the predictive direction. Use PLS or supervised selection if prediction is the goal.
- **Outliers:** variance is sensitive to outliers; outlier resistant PCA variants exist.
- **Interpretability:** components are mixtures of all features; signs are arbitrary.
- **Leakage:** fit inside the CV fold via a `Pipeline`.
- **Sparse data:** centring destroys sparsity; use `TruncatedSVD` instead.
Good uses: decorrelating features, compression, noise reduction (eigenfaces in CS229), speeding up and stabilising downstream models, first step before t-SNE or UMAP.
say: The main pitfalls: it's scale sensitive, so I standardise unless the features share units, otherwise large unit features dominate. It's linear, so curved structure isn't captured. It's unsupervised, so it keeps high variance directions, and a low variance direction can be exactly the one that predicts the target, which is why principal components regression can underperform. Variance is sensitive to outliers, components are hard to interpret, and their signs are arbitrary. In a pipeline it must be fit on the training fold only. For sparse data like text, centring destroys sparsity, so I'd use truncated SVD instead. It's great for decorrelating, compressing and denoising, and as a first step before t-SNE.

followups.q: Do you know any dimensionality reduction techniques besides PCA?
followups.a: LDA, truncated SVD, ICA, NMF, autoencoders, random projections, t-SNE and UMAP for visualisation.

followups.q: What is LDA as a dimensionality reduction method?
followups.a: A supervised projection that maximises between class relative to within class variance, giving at most K minus 1 dimensions.

source.title: Alexey Grigorev, data science interview theory questions

q: How does t-SNE work, and what are the common ways people misread t-SNE plots?
plain: The t-SNE method (t distributed stochastic neighbour embedding) makes a 2D map in which points that are close neighbours in the original high dimensional space stay close. The method turns distances into neighbour probabilities in both spaces and moves the 2D points until the two sets of probabilities match. Its perplexity setting is roughly how many neighbours each point considers, typically 5 to 50. The map preserves who is near whom, not sizes or far distances. Cluster sizes in the plot mean nothing, and gaps between clusters may mean nothing. Pure random noise can look like clusters at low perplexity. Always compare several perplexities and random seeds.
deep:
t-SNE: Gaussian affinities $p_{j\mid i}$ in the input space with bandwidth per point set by perplexity, symmetrised to $p_{ij}$; Student t (one degree of freedom) affinities $q_{ij} \propto (1 + \lVert y_i - y_j\rVert^2)^{-1}$ in 2D; minimise $\mathrm{KL}(P\,\Vert\,Q)$ by gradient descent. Heavy tails let dissimilar points separate (solving crowding).

Distill (Wattenberg, Viégas and Johnson, 2016):
- Hyperparameters matter: perplexity roughly 5 to 50 and below the number of points.
- Run to convergence; early stopping leaves pinched shapes.
- Cluster sizes mean nothing (dense regions expanded, sparse contracted).
- Distances between clusters may mean nothing.
- Random noise does not always look random.
- Some shapes are recoverable sometimes; topology may need several plots.
Classic t-SNE is non parametric (no transform for new points), stochastic, and $O(n^2)$ naive ($O(n\log n)$ with Barnes Hut).
say: t-SNE converts pairwise distances into neighbour probabilities, Gaussian in the original space with a per point width set by the perplexity, and Student t in the 2D map, and moves the map points to minimise the KL divergence between the two. The heavy tailed t distribution lets clusters separate. What it preserves is local neighbourhoods. The Distill article on reading t-SNE lists the traps: results change with perplexity, typically five to fifty; stopping early gives misleading shapes; cluster sizes mean nothing because dense regions get expanded; distances between clusters may mean nothing; and random noise can produce apparent clusters at low perplexity. So I compare several perplexities and seeds, and never treat plot geometry as measurement.
must_mention: cluster sizes and gaps are not meaningful

followups.q: Can you apply a fitted t-SNE to new points?
followups.a: Not in the classic algorithm; use parametric variants or UMAP's transform.

followups.q: Should you cluster on a t-SNE embedding?
followups.a: Only as exploration; validate any clusters in the original space.

traps: Reporting cluster sizes or inter cluster distances from a t-SNE plot as findings.

source.title: Wattenberg, Viégas and Johnson (2016), How to Use t-SNE Effectively

q: How does UMAP compare with t-SNE, and what do its main parameters do?
plain: UMAP (uniform manifold approximation and projection) also makes low dimensional maps that keep neighbours together. UMAP builds a graph of each point's nearest neighbours and lays it out. That approach is usually much faster than t-SNE (t distributed stochastic neighbour embedding, an earlier mapping method). UMAP also scales to larger data and to more than two output dimensions. The n_neighbors setting, default 15, trades fine local detail for broader structure: 2 gives disconnected fragments, and a few hundred shows the big picture. The min_dist setting, default 0.1, controls how tightly points pack, with 0 giving tight clumps. Unlike classic t-SNE, a fitted UMAP can place new points. The same warning applies: sizes and gaps in the picture are not measurements.
deep:
UMAP: weighted k nearest neighbour graph (fuzzy simplicial set) in the input space; optimise a low dimensional layout with a cross entropy objective between graph weights.

Parameters (umap-learn docs):
- `n_neighbors` (15): local versus global; 2 yields many disconnected components, 200 preserves broad structure but loses detail.
- `min_dist` (0.1): minimum spacing; 0.0 for clustering style clumps, up to 0.99 for spread out views.
- `n_components` (2): scales well to 10 or 50 for downstream clustering, unlike t-SNE.
- `metric` ("euclidean"): cosine, Manhattan, precomputed, custom numba functions.

Versus t-SNE: faster, supports `transform` for new data, often described as keeping more global structure, but distances and densities are still distorted; both are stochastic; inspect multiple settings.
say: Both are neighbour preserving embeddings, but UMAP builds a weighted k nearest neighbour graph and optimises a layout that matches it, which is generally faster than t-SNE, scales to more output dimensions, and supports transforming new points. n_neighbors, default fifteen, is the local versus global knob: very small values fragment the data into disconnected pieces, large values keep broad structure at the cost of detail. min_dist, default 0.1, controls how tightly points pack, so zero gives tight clumps useful for clustering. People say UMAP preserves global structure better, but I'd still treat cluster sizes and gaps as unreliable and check results across several settings and seeds.

followups.q: Which would you use for 10 dimensional embeddings feeding a clusterer?
followups.a: UMAP, since it scales with n_components; t-SNE is designed for 2 or 3.

followups.q: Why do both distort densities?
followups.a: They normalise local neighbourhoods so dense and sparse regions take similar space.

source.title: UMAP documentation: basic parameters

q: What is a confusion matrix, and what are precision and recall?
plain: A confusion matrix counts a classifier's four outcomes. True positives are flagged and real, and false positives are flagged but not real. False negatives are missed real cases, and true negatives are correctly left alone. Precision asks, of everything I flagged, what share was real. If you flag 20 transactions as fraud and 8 are truly fraud, precision is 0.4. Recall asks, of all real cases, what share did I catch. If there were 10 frauds, recall is 0.8. Precision matters when false alarms are costly, and recall matters when misses are costly.
deep:
| | Predicted positive | Predicted negative |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Actual positive | TP | FN |
| Actual negative | FP | TN |

- Precision (positive predictive value) $= \frac{TP}{TP + FP}$.
- Recall (sensitivity, true positive rate) $= \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$.
- Specificity (true negative rate) $= \frac{TN}{TN + FP}$; false positive rate $= 1 -$ specificity.
- Accuracy $= \frac{TP + TN}{\text{total}}$.
Precision depends on prevalence; recall and specificity do not. All depend on the decision threshold.
say: The confusion matrix tabulates predictions against truth: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives. Precision is TP over TP plus FP, the fraction of my positive predictions that are correct, so it answers how much I can trust a flag. Recall is TP over TP plus FN, the fraction of actual positives I catch. In fraud, if I flag twenty transactions and eight are fraud, precision is 0.4; if there were ten frauds, recall is 0.8. Which one matters depends on costs: a cancer screen prioritises recall, a spam filter that hides real email prioritises precision. Both depend on the threshold, and precision also depends on prevalence.
must_mention: precision TP over TP plus FP
recall TP over TP plus FN

followups.q: What are the cells in the confusion table?
followups.a: True positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives.

followups.q: What is specificity?
followups.a: TN over TN plus FP, the share of negatives correctly left alone.

source.title: Alexey Grigorev, data science interview theory questions

q: Compute precision, recall, F1 and accuracy from a confusion matrix, and explain why accuracy can mislead.
plain: Take 100 cases with 10 real positives, where the model flags 20 and catches 8 of the 10. So true positives are 8, false positives 12, false negatives 2, and true negatives 78. Precision is 8 out of 20, which is 0.4, and recall is 8 out of 10, which is 0.8. F1 (the balance of precision and recall) is 0.533, and accuracy is 86 out of 100, which is 0.86. But predicting no for everyone scores 0.90 accuracy. So this genuinely useful model looks worse than doing nothing. That is why a cancer detector boasting 99.99 percent accuracy tells you nothing until you know how rare cancer is in the data.
deep:
TP 8, FP 12, FN 2, TN 78 (verified with sklearn):
- Precision $8/20 = 0.4$; recall $8/10 = 0.8$; F1 $= 2(0.4)(0.8)/1.2 = 0.533$; accuracy $86/100 = 0.86$.
- Majority baseline accuracy $= 0.90$.

Accuracy paradox: with prevalence $\pi$, the constant negative classifier has accuracy $1 - \pi$; at 0.01 percent prevalence, 99.99 percent accuracy is achievable with zero recall. Always report the baseline, recall, precision, and a threshold free metric (PR AUC). Balanced accuracy (mean of recall and specificity) or Matthews correlation are alternatives that account for imbalance.
say: With a hundred cases and ten positives, suppose the model flags twenty and eight are right. So TP is 8, FP 12, FN 2 and TN 78. Precision is 8 over 20, 0.4; recall is 8 over 10, 0.8; F1 is two times 0.4 times 0.8 over 1.2, about 0.53; accuracy is 0.86. The trap is that predicting negative for everyone gets 0.90 accuracy, so accuracy ranks the useless model above the useful one. That's my answer to a colleague claiming a cancer model is solved at 99.99 percent accuracy: compare it with the majority baseline and look at recall and precision, because with rare positives accuracy is dominated by the negatives.
must_mention: use recall, precision, PR AUC under imbalance

followups.q: Is accuracy always a good metric?
followups.a: No; under class imbalance or unequal costs it hides failure on the minority class.

followups.q: How could this model be improved?
followups.a: Tune the threshold for the cost trade off, add features, or reweight classes; check PR AUC across thresholds.

source.title: Chip Huyen, ML Interviews Book, objectives, metrics and evaluation

q: What is the F1 score, what is F beta, and how do you average F1 over several classes?
plain: F1 is the harmonic mean (an average dragged toward the lower value) of precision and recall, which stays low unless both are decent. Precision 0.9 with recall 0.1 gives an F1 of only 0.18, while their plain average would be 0.5. F beta lets you weight recall beta times as much as precision. So F2 favours recall, which is useful for screening. With several classes, macro averaging computes F1 per class and averages them equally, so rare classes count as much as common ones. Micro averaging pools all counts first, which for ordinary single label problems equals accuracy. Always predicting positive at 1 percent prevalence gives F1 of just 0.0198.
deep:
$F_1 = \frac{2PR}{P + R} = \frac{2TP}{2TP + FP + FN}$; $F_\beta = (1 + \beta^2)\frac{PR}{\beta^2P + R}$.

Advantages over accuracy: ignores true negatives, so it is not inflated by a dominant negative class. Weaknesses: ignores TN entirely, depends on the threshold and on which class is called positive, and is not symmetric.

Multiclass: macro (unweighted mean of per class F1), weighted (by support), micro (global TP, FP, FN; equals accuracy for single label multiclass).

Worked: always predicting positive at prevalence $p$ gives precision $p$, recall 1, $F_1 = 2p/(1 + p)$, which is 0.0198 at $p = 0.01$ (verified). If the minority class is labelled 0 instead, F1 of the majority class is near 0.995, so the labelling choice changes the number.
say: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, two P R over P plus R, so it's high only when both are high; precision 0.9 and recall 0.1 gives about 0.18. Unlike accuracy it ignores true negatives, which is why it's popular under imbalance, though it depends on the threshold and on which class you call positive. F beta weights recall beta times as much, so F2 suits screening where misses are worse. For multiclass, macro F1 averages per class scores equally, which highlights rare classes; weighted averages by support; micro pools counts and equals accuracy for single label problems. As a sanity check, always predicting positive at one percent prevalence gives F1 of only about 0.02.
must_mention: harmonic mean of precision and recall
depends on threshold and positive class

followups.q: Can F1 be used for more than two classes?
followups.a: Yes, via macro, micro or weighted averaging of per class F1.

followups.q: With a 99 to 1 split, what is F1 if the model always predicts the majority class?
followups.a: Zero for the minority class as positive; about 0.995 if the majority class is treated as positive.

source.title: Chip Huyen, ML Interviews Book, objectives, metrics and evaluation

q: What is the precision recall trade off?
plain: Most classifiers output a score, and you choose a threshold above which you say yes. Raising the threshold makes the model flag fewer cases. So the flags are more often right (higher precision), but more real cases slip through (lower recall). Lowering the threshold catches more real cases but with more false alarms. A fraud team that can review only 100 alerts a day would set the threshold so the top 100 scores are flagged. That team accepts whatever recall that gives. The precision recall curve shows every possible trade off at once.
deep:
For threshold $t$: predict positive if $s(x) \ge t$. As $t$ increases, TP and FP both fall; recall is non increasing in $t$, precision usually rises but not monotonically (it can dip when a true positive drops out). The PR curve plots precision against recall over all $t$; its area (average precision) summarises it.

Choosing the operating point: from costs (expected cost minimisation), a recall target (catch 95 percent of fraud), a precision target, a capacity constraint (top $k$ per day), or maximum $F_\beta$, all on validation data. Report test metrics at the frozen threshold.
say: A classifier gives scores, and the threshold turns scores into decisions. If I raise the threshold, I flag fewer cases: the ones I flag are more likely correct, so precision tends to go up, but I miss more true positives, so recall goes down. Lowering it does the reverse. The precision recall curve traces this across all thresholds. Which point I pick is a business decision: a recall target for medical screening, a precision target when false alarms are expensive, or a capacity constraint like a team that can review a hundred cases a day. I pick the threshold on validation data and report test metrics at that fixed threshold.
must_mention: higher threshold raises precision lowers recall
PR curve shows all trade offs
operating point from costs or capacity

followups.q: Is precision monotone in the threshold?
followups.a: Not strictly; it can dip when a true positive falls below the threshold.

followups.q: How would you pick a threshold with no explicit costs?
followups.a: Maximise F1 or F beta on validation data, or meet a recall or capacity target.

source.title: Alexey Grigorev, data science interview theory questions

q: What is the ROC curve, and what does ROC AUC mean?
plain: The ROC (receiver operating characteristic) curve plots the true positive rate (recall) against the false positive rate as the decision threshold sweeps from high to low. A perfect classifier hugs the top left corner. Random guessing follows the diagonal. The area under the ROC curve is called the AUC (area under the curve). The AUC has a clean meaning: the probability that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative. So an AUC of 0.85 means that 85 percent of positive and negative pairs are ranked correctly. The AUC measures ranking quality only, not whether the probabilities are accurate.
deep:
TPR $= TP/(TP + FN)$, FPR $= FP/(FP + TN)$, plotted for all thresholds.

$$\mathrm{AUC} = P(s(X^+) > s(X^-)) + \tfrac12P(s(X^+) = s(X^-)),$$
the normalised Mann Whitney U statistic. Verified: sklearn's ROC AUC of 0.850 equalled the pairwise ranking probability 0.850.

Properties: 0.5 for random, 1 for perfect, below 0.5 means inverted ranking; invariant to monotone transforms of the score (so it ignores calibration); invariant to class prevalence (TPR and FPR are each normalised within a class). Partial AUC focuses on the low FPR region that matters in screening.
say: The ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate as I sweep the threshold, from flagging nothing at the bottom left to flagging everything at the top right. The area under it has a nice probabilistic meaning: it's the probability that a randomly chosen positive is scored above a randomly chosen negative, which is the Mann Whitney statistic; in a quick check sklearn's AUC matched that pairwise probability exactly. So 0.5 is random ranking and 1 is perfect. Because it only depends on ranking, it's invariant to any monotone transform of the scores, so it says nothing about calibration, and it doesn't change with class prevalence.
must_mention: AUC equals P of positive scored above negative

followups.q: What is the ROC curve, and when do you use it?
followups.a: TPR versus FPR across thresholds; use AUC to compare rankers, especially across populations with different prevalence.

followups.q: How do you interpret an AUC of 0.7?
followups.a: A random positive outranks a random negative 70 percent of the time.

source.title: Alexey Grigorev, data science interview theory questions

q: When is PR AUC better than ROC AUC? Explain with class imbalance.
plain: PR AUC (the area under the precision recall curve) is better than ROC AUC (the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) when positives are rare. ROC AUC uses the false positive rate, which divides false alarms by the huge number of negatives. So even thousands of false alarms look small when negatives dominate. Precision instead compares false alarms with true finds, so it shows how bad things really are. In a test with identical score distributions, ROC AUC stayed at 0.85 whether positives were 50 percent or 1 percent of the data. Over the same range, PR AUC fell from 0.85 to 0.14. When positives are rare and false alarms cost money, as in fraud or disease screening, PR AUC is the more honest summary.
deep:
Prevalence $\pi$: precision $= \frac{\mathrm{TPR}\,\pi}{\mathrm{TPR}\,\pi + \mathrm{FPR}(1 - \pi)}$, so the same ROC point gives very different precision as $\pi$ falls. A random classifier's PR AUC equals $\pi$.

Verified: same Gaussian scores, prevalence 0.50 gives ROC AUC 0.850 and AP 0.846; prevalence 0.01 gives ROC AUC 0.853 and AP 0.138.

Saito and Rehmsmeier (PLOS ONE, 2015): 500 true positives cost 160 false positives with balanced data but 1,600 with ten times more negatives; precision at 50 percent recall falls from 75 to 25 percent while the ROC curve is unchanged. Use ROC AUC to compare ranking across populations; PR AUC (average precision), precision at fixed recall, or precision at $k$ when positives are rare.
say: Under heavy imbalance ROC AUC can look great while the model is useless in practice, because the false positive rate is normalised by the large number of negatives: one percent FPR on a million negatives is ten thousand false alarms. Precision counts false positives against true positives, so it reflects what a reviewer actually experiences. In a simulation with the same score distributions, ROC AUC was about 0.85 at both fifty percent and one percent prevalence, while average precision dropped from 0.85 to 0.14. Saito and Rehmsmeier make the same point. So for rare positives with costly false alarms I'd report PR AUC or precision at a fixed recall, and keep ROC AUC for comparing ranking across populations.
must_mention: ROC AUC unchanged, PR AUC collapses
use PR AUC for rare costly positives

followups.q: In which cases is AU PR better than AU ROC?
followups.a: When positives are rare and the cost of false positives relative to true positives matters.

followups.q: What is the PR AUC of a random classifier?
followups.a: The positive rate, for example 0.01 at one percent prevalence.

source.title: Saito and Rehmsmeier (2015), PLOS ONE

q: How is the PR curve summarised, and why shouldn't you linearly interpolate it?
plain: The usual summary of a precision recall curve is average precision. Average precision is the precision at each threshold, weighted by how much recall increases there, summed up. Average precision behaves like the area under the curve but is computed from the actual steps. Connecting PR (precision recall) points with straight lines, as you would on a ROC (receiver operating characteristic) curve, overstates performance. Precision does not change linearly between two operating points. A random model's PR curve sits at the positive rate, not at 0.5. So a PR AUC (area under the curve) of 0.2 can be good if only 1 percent of cases are positive.
deep:
Average precision: $\mathrm{AP} = \sum_n(R_n - R_{n-1})P_n$ (sklearn `average_precision_score`), a step function summary without interpolation.

Interpolation: between ROC points linear interpolation is achievable by randomising between classifiers; in PR space the achievable curve between points A and B is non linear (Saito and Rehmsmeier give $y = \frac{TP_A + x}{TP_A + x + FP_A + \frac{FP_B - FP_A}{TP_B - TP_A}x}$), and the trapezoidal rule in PR space is optimistic.

Baseline: $\pi = P/(P + N)$. Compare PR AUC with the baseline, or report lift ($\mathrm{AP}/\pi$). Ties in scores and the handling of the first point also matter.
say: I summarise a PR curve with average precision, which sums precision at each threshold weighted by the increase in recall, a step function with no interpolation. That matters because, unlike ROC space, you can't linearly interpolate between two PR points: the achievable precision between two operating points is a non linear curve, and the trapezoid rule overestimates the area. Saito and Rehmsmeier discuss this and give the correct interpolation formula. The other thing I always state is the baseline: a random classifier's PR AUC equals the positive rate, so I'd report average precision alongside prevalence, or as a lift, rather than comparing it to 0.5.
must_mention: no linear interpolation in PR space

followups.q: What is the area under the PR curve useful for?
followups.a: Comparing classifiers on rare positive problems; report it with the prevalence baseline.

followups.q: What is the PR curve?
followups.a: Precision against recall over all thresholds.

source.title: Saito and Rehmsmeier (2015), PLOS ONE

q: What are log loss and the Brier score, and what is a proper scoring rule?
plain: Log loss scores predicted probabilities by the negative log of the probability given to what actually happened. Predicting 0.5 always costs 0.69 per case, while one confident miss at 0.01 costs 4.6. The Brier score is the average squared difference between the predicted probability and the outcome, which is 0 or 1. Always predicting the 10 percent base rate on a 10 percent problem scores 0.09. Both are proper scoring rules, meaning you get the best expected score only by reporting your true beliefs. So proper scoring rules reward honest probabilities. Log loss punishes confident mistakes far more harshly than Brier.
deep:
Log loss $= -\frac1n\sum_i[y_i\log p_i + (1 - y_i)\log(1 - p_i)]$ (verified: 0.6931 for constant 0.5; 4.605 for $p = 0.01$ on a positive). Unbounded; clip probabilities in practice.

Brier $= \frac1n\sum_i(p_i - y_i)^2 \in [0, 1]$ (verified: 0.09 for constant 0.1 at 10 percent prevalence).

Strictly proper: expected score is uniquely optimised by the true probability. Murphy decomposition: Brier $=$ reliability $-$ resolution $+$ uncertainty, so a lower Brier score can come from better discrimination even if calibration is worse (sklearn calibration guide); to judge calibration alone, look at the reliability term or a reliability diagram. Accuracy and F1 are not proper scoring rules for probabilities.
say: Log loss is the average negative log probability assigned to the true outcome, so a constant fifty percent prediction costs ln two, about 0.69, and a single confident miss at one percent costs about 4.6, which is why log loss is brutal on overconfidence. The Brier score is the mean squared error between probability and outcome, bounded between zero and one; predicting the base rate of ten percent on a ten percent problem scores 0.09. Both are strictly proper scoring rules, meaning the expected score is optimised only by reporting the true probability. One nuance: a better Brier score doesn't prove better calibration, because it also rewards discrimination; the Murphy decomposition separates the two.
must_mention: log loss negative log probability of truth

followups.q: Why prefer log loss over Brier, or vice versa?
followups.a: Log loss heavily penalises confident errors and matches likelihood training; Brier is bounded and less sensitive to extreme mistakes.

followups.q: How do you measure how close a learned distribution Q is to the true P?
followups.a: KL divergence, or in practice cross entropy, which differs from KL by the entropy of P.

source.title: scikit-learn: probability calibration

q: What does it mean for a classifier to be calibrated, and how do you check it?
plain: A classifier is calibrated if its probabilities mean what they say: among all cases given a 0.8 chance, about 80 percent should turn out positive. You check this with a reliability diagram. Group predictions into bins by predicted probability, then plot the actual positive rate in each bin against the average prediction. A calibrated model follows the diagonal. Different models fail in typical ways. Naive Bayes is overconfident, pushing toward 0 and 1. Random forests are underconfident at the extremes, because averaging many trees rarely gives unanimous votes. Logistic regression is usually close to calibrated.
deep:
Calibrated: $P(Y = 1\mid \hat p(X) = p) = p$ for all $p$.

Reliability diagram (`CalibrationDisplay`, `calibration_curve`): bin $\hat p$, plot observed frequency against mean predicted probability, with a histogram of predictions. Summary metrics: expected calibration error (weighted mean gap across bins), the Brier reliability term.

Typical shapes (sklearn calibration guide): logistic regression close to the diagonal (log loss is proper and its link matches it); GaussianNB pushes toward 0 and 1 (redundant features double counted); random forests form a sigmoid, rarely near 0 or 1 (Niculescu Mizil and Caruana's explanation: averaging high variance trees); LinearSVC even more sigmoidal (max margin focuses on the boundary). Boosted trees with log loss are often reasonable but should still be checked. Class weighting and resampling distort calibration.
say: Calibration means the predicted probabilities match observed frequencies: of the cases scored around 0.8, about eighty percent are positive. I check it with a reliability diagram, binning predictions and plotting the observed positive rate against the mean predicted probability, plus a histogram showing where predictions concentrate; I might also report expected calibration error. Typical patterns from scikit-learn's calibration guide: logistic regression is usually close to the diagonal, naive Bayes is overconfident, random forests are pulled away from zero and one, and SVMs give a pronounced sigmoid shape. It matters whenever probabilities drive decisions, like expected cost thresholds or pricing, and class weighting or resampling will distort it.
must_mention: random forests pulled from the extremes

followups.q: Why are random forest probabilities rarely near 0 or 1?
followups.a: Averaging many high variance trees means unanimous votes are rare, pulling predictions toward the middle.

followups.q: Does calibration affect ROC AUC?
followups.a: Not for strictly monotone recalibration; isotonic regression can create ties that change it slightly.

source.title: scikit-learn: probability calibration

q: How do you calibrate a classifier? Compare Platt scaling and isotonic regression.
plain: Calibration fits a small mapping from the model's raw scores to better probabilities. You fit the mapping using data the model was not trained on, because a model is overconfident on its own training data. Platt scaling fits an S shaped logistic curve to the scores. Platt scaling has only two parameters, so it works with small calibration sets and keeps the ranking unchanged. Isotonic regression fits any steadily increasing step function, so it can fix any distortion shape. Isotonic regression needs more data, roughly a thousand or more calibration examples, or it overfits. For many classes, temperature scaling divides all scores by one learned number.
deep:
`CalibratedClassifierCV(estimator, method=..., cv=k)`:
- `ensemble=True`: per fold, train on $k - 1$ folds and fit the calibrator on the held out fold; average the $k$ pairs. `ensemble=False`: one calibrator on out of fold predictions, refit the model on all data.
- `FrozenEstimator` wraps an already fitted model to calibrate on separate held out data.

Methods (sklearn guide):
- **Sigmoid (Platt):** $p = 1/(1 + \exp(Af + B))$; good for small samples and symmetric, sigmoid shaped distortion; strictly monotone, preserves AUC; can fail for very imbalanced problems.
- **Isotonic:** non parametric non decreasing fit minimising squared error; as good or better than sigmoid with more than about 1,000 samples; overfits small sets; ties can change AUC.
- **Temperature scaling** (listed in the current guide): $\mathrm{softmax}(z/T)$ with one parameter fit by log loss; multiclass, leaves the argmax and accuracy unchanged.
Evaluate with log loss, Brier and reliability diagrams on a further held out set.
say: I fit a calibrator that maps the model's scores to probabilities on data the model didn't train on, typically with CalibratedClassifierCV, which handles the cross fitting. Platt scaling fits a logistic curve with two parameters to the scores; it's data efficient, strictly monotone so it preserves ranking and AUC, and suits the sigmoid shaped distortion typical of SVMs and forests. Isotonic regression fits any monotone step function, so it can correct arbitrary distortions, but it overfits small calibration sets; scikit-learn's guide suggests it's as good or better beyond about a thousand samples. For multiclass, temperature scaling divides the logits by one learned temperature, leaving accuracy unchanged. Then I verify with a reliability diagram on fresh data.
must_mention: Platt fits a two parameter sigmoid
isotonic fits a monotone step function
isotonic needs roughly a thousand samples

followups.q: Why not calibrate on the training data?
followups.a: The model is overconfident on data it has seen, so the calibrator would learn the wrong mapping.

followups.q: Does calibration change accuracy?
followups.a: Monotone calibration preserves ranking; with a fixed 0.5 threshold, predicted labels can change.

source.title: scikit-learn: probability calibration

q: Which regression metrics do you know? When would you use RMSE instead of MAE, or MAPE?
plain: RMSE (root mean squared error) is the square root of the average squared error. RMSE punishes big misses heavily, so one error of 10 counts as much as a hundred errors of 1. Use RMSE when large errors are disproportionately bad. MAE (mean absolute error), the average absolute error, treats every unit of error equally and is less swayed by a few outliers. MAE is minimised by predicting the median. MAPE (mean absolute percentage error) expresses errors as percentages, which is handy across products with different scales. But MAPE breaks when actual values are near zero, and MAPE penalises over prediction more than under prediction. R squared compares the model with always predicting the mean.
deep:
| Metric | Formula | Optimal constant | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MSE / RMSE | $\frac1n\sum e_i^2$, its root | mean | Gaussian likelihood; outlier sensitive; RMSE in target units |
| MAE | $\frac1n\sum\lvert e_i\rvert$ | median | Laplace likelihood; resistant to outliers |
| MAPE | $\frac{100}{n}\sum\lvert e_i/y_i\rvert$ | biased low | undefined at $y = 0$; asymmetric |
| sMAPE, WAPE | scaled variants | | fix some MAPE issues |
| Pinball (quantile $\tau$) | $\sum\max(\tau e, (\tau - 1)e)$ | $\tau$ quantile | prediction intervals |
| $R^2$ | $1 - \mathrm{SSR}/\mathrm{SST}$ | | relative to the mean; can be negative out of sample |
| Huber | quadratic then linear | | compromise loss |

Match the training loss to the metric where possible, and report errors at the deployed horizon or granularity.
say: The common ones are MSE and RMSE, MAE, MAPE, R squared, and quantile loss. RMSE squares errors, so it's minimised by the conditional mean and heavily penalises large misses; I use it when one big error is worse than many small ones. MAE is minimised by the median and is more resistant to outliers, so it suits skewed targets or when every unit of error costs the same. MAPE is scale free, which helps compare products, but it's undefined at zero and asymmetric, punishing over forecasts more. R squared tells me improvement over predicting the mean. If the business needs intervals, I'd use quantile loss. Ideally the training loss matches the evaluation metric.
must_mention: RMSE penalises large errors, optimal at the mean
MAE resistant to outliers, optimal at the median
MAPE scale free but breaks near zero
R squared relative to the mean

followups.q: When should you use RMSE instead of MAE?
followups.a: When large errors are disproportionately costly or the noise is roughly Gaussian.

followups.q: You must predict a price 8 hours ahead and never be off by more than 10 percent. Which metric?
followups.a: A percentage error such as MAPE, or the maximum absolute percentage error if the bound is strict.

source.title: Chip Huyen, ML Interviews Book, objectives, metrics and evaluation

q: How do you choose a classification threshold from the costs of errors?
plain: If your probabilities are calibrated, the cheapest decision is to flag a case whenever ignoring it is expected to cost more than flagging it. That works out to flagging when the probability is above the false positive cost divided by the sum of both costs. If a missed fraud costs 10 times a false alarm, the threshold is 1 divided by 11, about 0.09, not 0.5. Without explicit costs, pick the threshold on validation data to hit a recall target, fill a daily review capacity, or maximise F1. Then freeze the threshold before testing.
deep:
Predict positive iff $p\,c_{FN} > (1 - p)\,c_{FP}$, i.e.
$$p > t^\star = \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}}.$$
